notes.full_text:
Fluid is hypoechoic (black). Vessels are round black structures that can be traced proximally and distally confirming their continuous tubular structure. Short axis imaging is much easier than long axis.
Acoustic enhancement (a small, brighter, whiter area) is usually seen immediately deep to vessels. This is due to a reduction of ultrasound attenuation as it passes through the fluid as compared to the surrounding tissue.
A torniquet will fill veins for easier imaging and vascular access. Use light probe pressure to avoid compressing veins, especially small, superficial veins.
The easiest and fastest way to differentiate vein from artery and confirm vein patency is simple compression with the probe. Veins will fully collapse, excluding thrombosis. Arterial pulsations are made more obvious by partially compressing the vessel.
Colour flow doppler can also be used to confirm flow in a vein. Tilting the probe to align flow towards or away from the probe is required for colour flow. (BART: blue away, red towards). Distal compression (squeeze the limb distally) augments flow and is a good sign to confirm vessel is a vein and its patency. Power doppler is more sensitive for low flow but does not show direction. It is useful for small veins with slow flow.
Larger central veins can pulsate. Valves may sometimes be seen in veins especially larger veins.

acoustic enhancement deep to vessels.

notes.full_text:
Fluid is hypoechoic (black). Vessels are round black structures that can be traced proximally and distally confirming their continuous tubular structure. Short axis imaging is much easier than long axis.
Acoustic enhancement (a small, brighter, whiter area) is usually seen immediately deep to vessels. This is due to a reduction of ultrasound attenuation as it passes through the fluid as compared to the surrounding tissue.
The easiest and fastest way to confirm an artery from a vein is simple compression with the probe. Veins will easily fully collapse. Arteries are more difficult to compress and arterial pulsations are made more obvious by partial compression.
Arteries have thicker walls, smaller lumens and are more rounded in shape than veins. The thicker wall is usually seen as intima (white) and media (black) and adventitia (white) at the 12 O’clock and 6 O’clock positions. This appearance is because the axial resolution of our ultrasound probes is generally better than lateral resolution. Atheroma may thicken and calcify arterial walls further, making the actual lumen much smaller than it initially appears. Compression and colour can help to clarify the actual lumen.
Use colour doppler to confirm pulsatile flow (beware large central veins can sometimes also have pulsatile flow.) Tilting the probe to align flow towards or away from the probe is required for colour doppler. ( BART: blue away, red towards). Arteries often run in a neurovascular bundle with accompanying veins and nerves.

notes.full_text:
Peripheral nerves are easiest imaged in short axis. They typically appear as a hyperechoic (whitish) rounded structures containing hypoechoic (blackish) round fascicles of varying size and number. Usually described as a “honeycomb” appearance. The white areas are connective tissue and epineurium around and between fascicles, and the black areas are the nerve fascicles. The proximal roots of the brachial plexus are an exception to this as they appear as hypoechoic, circular structures similar to vessels due to a lack of connective tissue and the nerve root being all nerve axons. Very small peripheral nerves may also contain only a single hypoechoic fascicle.
Nerves should be traced proximally and distally to confirm their continuous nature, and expected anatomical relations. This is essential to differentiate them from other similar appearing round structures like lymph nodes and tendons. Nerves usually travel in fascial planes between muscles, often with vessels nearby. Although usually cylindrical, nerves can sometimes have a very flattened structure, e.g. the femoral nerve. Nerves are anisotropic, meaning tilting the probe to ensure the ultrasound beam is perpendicular to the nerve surface will result in a brighter, whiter appearance. Tilting the probe away from perpendicular to the nerve surface will result in a darker, blacker appearance.
Long axis imaging is more difficult. This will show the hyperechoic nerve with multiple parallel hypoechoic fascicles. Often described as a "corduroy" appearance.
Compared with tendons nerves have a fascicular appearance with variable sized and numbers of round, hypoechoic fascicles. Tendons have a fibrillar appearance which is a finer, more homogenous speckled appearance as compared to the more discrete, variable sized fascicles in nerves. Tendons are more anisotropic, and when traced they change size and appearance as they expand into muscles or insert into bones.

notes.full_text: Tendons are hyperechoic (whitish) and anisotropic (brightness changes with probe tilting) with a “fibrillar” appearance. They can easily be misidentified as nerves. Tendons can be rounded but are often more oval or flatter than nerves. Tracing the structure proximally and distally is the most reliable way to distinguish tendons from nerves. While nerves are continuous, cylindrical structures with expected anatomical relations, tendons dramatically change shape as they are traced proximally and distally. Tendons usually expand into a muscle belly or appear to “dissolve” into the middle of a muscle belly. With high resolution probes the finer, more homogenous “fibrillar” appearance of tendons can be distinguished from the more discrete, irregular “fascicular” appearance of nerves. Tendon movement can also be elucidated by moving the relevant muscle.

notes.full_text:
Nerves Vs Tendons notes
Tendons can easily be misidentified as nerves. Tracing the structure proximally and distally is the most reliable way to distinguish tendons from nerves. Nerves are continuous, cylindrical structures, usually running in fascial planes, with branches and expected anatomical relations. Tendons dramatically change size and shape as they are traced proximally, usually expanding into a muscle belly or appearing to “dissolve” into the middle of a muscle belly, or inserting into bone distally.
Tendons can be rounded but are often more oval or flatter than nerves and tend not to branch. Tendon movement can also be elucidated by moving the relevant muscle.
With high resolution probes the finer, more homogenous “fibrillar” appearance of tendons can be distinguished from the more discrete, irregular “fascicular” appearance of nerves.

notes.full_text:
Muscles are mostly large hypoechoic structures, enclosed in fibrous fascial sheaths, often creating defined layers on the US image. They have variable texture depending on age and ratios of muscle fibres: connective tissue: fat within the muscle.
The muscle fibres are hypoechoic with the perimysium surrounding the muscle fibres appearing hyperechoic. In short axis this produces a “starry night” appearance and in long axis multiple parallel hyperechoic strands. The direction of the muscle fibres varies with muscle structure and function. Often muscles are imaged obliquely as we focus on imaging nerves or vessels. This produces an appearance of multiple parallel short hyperechoic strands through the muscle.
Tracing muscles shows their shape to change dramatically often forming tendons, peripheral aponeurosis, or inserting into bone.
Muscles are anisotropic, so the brightness of their ultrasound appearance changes with tilting of the probe.

notes.full_text:
Subcutaneous fat notes
Fat appears mostly hypoechoic. It contains variable amounts of hyperechoic fibrous strands and septa that are not as organised or as homogenous as in muscle. These septa can form fat filled compartments within fat layers. Fat layers often contain vessels and small nerves, frequently in these septated compartments. Fat layers are also usually continuous and do not usually form defined structures enclosed in fascial sheaths, unlike muscles. Fat is most commonly seen in the subcutaneous layer, in fascial planes and around viscera.

notes.full_text: Bone does not transmit US. As all US is reflected bone appears as a bright hyperechoic cortex with a hypoechoic acoustic shadow deep to the cortex extending to the bottom of the image. Hence no image of bone medulla, opposite bone cortex or any structures deep to the bone will appear. Commonly various reverberation artefacts may be seen within the acoustic shadow. These are generated by the strongly reflective bone cortex and reflective structures above the bone that the US waves can bounce between resulting in a falsely appearing deeper structure within the bone acoustic shadow.

notes.full_text: Joints appear as hypoechoic spaces between the hyperechoic bone cortex of adjacent bones. Joints contain hypoechoic cartilage immediately covering cortex and hypoechoic synovial fluid in joint spaces.

notes.full_text: Fascial planes appear as hyperechoic, anisotropic, linear structures forming boundaries to fat layers and between muscles. They commonly contain loose connective tissue and potential spaces that vessels and nerves run in. These potential spaces can be opened and filled with local anaesthetic to surround nerves running in these planes.

layers.name: Acoustic shadow and reverberation artefacts from pleura-air interface

notes.full_text:
US is not transmitted in air, so normal aerated lung cannot be imaged. Lung US is mostly about artefacts generated from the pleura and imaging pathology that produces fluid in the lungs.
Normal lung appears as a hyperechoic pleura that slides back and forth with normal respiration. No detail of lung deep to pleura is imaged due to the air. A lines are a type of reverberation artefact generated between probe and pleura that are seen in normal lung.
Pleura is best imaged with a linear probe with the ultrasound beam directed perpendicular to the pleura. Imaging the ribs in short axis makes identifying pleura easier between, and just deep to the ribs.
A curvilinear or phased array probe is used for deeper lung and artefact imaging.

notes.full_text: Small bowel may be seen when imaging the abdominal wall. Deep to the abdominal wall muscles the peritoneum, solid viscera, bowel and mesentery will be seen. Ascending and descending colon have fixed positions in the lateral abdomen and transverse colon is usually located in the upper abdomen. Small bowel is mobile but usually located centrally in the abdomen. Small bowel generally appears as a thin walled rounded structure containing fluid with some solids. Hypoechoic bowel wall and plicae circularis (folds of bowel wall) may be seen with high frequency probes in thin subjects. Compared to large bowel small bowel has a smaller lumen, often contains fluid (hypoechoic) with particulate matter ( hyperechoic) and peristaltic movements are prominent and usually seen. Small bowel has plicae circularis ( thin folds of mucosa close together) while large bowel has hausta( larger sacular pouches of bowel wall further apart).

notes.full_text: Large bowel may be seen when imaging the abdominal wall. Deep to the abdominal wall muscles the peritoneum, solid viscera, bowel and mesentery can be seen. Ascending and descending colon have fixed positions in the lateral abdomen while transverse colon is variably located in the upper abdomen. Large bowel generally appears as a thin walled rounded structure containing air and solids. Hypoechoic bowel wall may be seen with high frequency probes in thin subjects. Compared with small bowel, large bowel peristalsis is slow and not usually seen. Large bowel has a larger lumen with haustral folds, contains hyperechoic solids, and usually contains air. The air results in a prominent air interface with acoustic shadowing below often with artefacts which produces a “rainclouds” appearance.

notes.full_text:
Axillary brachial plexus notes
Indications: anaesthesia to hand. Anaesthesia to forearm if musculocutaneous and medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm are successfully blocked with this technique (sometimes missed with this technique due to incorrect identification and anatomical variations). Analgesia to whole arm below the shoulder joint.
Positioning: supine with arm abducted 90º.
Volume: 20 mL, (5 mL per nerve).
Side effects: muscle weakness of arm and hand.
Complications: vessel puncture, intravascular injection and LAST, nerve injury.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe high in the axilla at the level of the pectoralis major/biceps groove, imaging the arm in a transverse view towards the humerus. Identify the axillary artery very superficially and the deeper, straight hyperechoic line of the fascia covering the conjoint tendon (from latissimus dorsi and teres major). This should be a straight hyperechoic fascia posterior to the artery which extends from superficial to a deep anterior attachment on the humerus. If you do not see this you are likely too distal, slide more proximally.
Three nerves sit adjacent to the artery. The median nerve is usually superficial and anterior (12-3 o’clock to artery), the ulnar nerve superficial and posterior (9-12 o’clock), the radial nerve deep and posterior (7-10 o’clock) between the artery and the conjoint tendon fascia. The smaller medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm may also be seen superficial to the artery, usually within the axillary sheath between median and ulnar nerves. The musculocutaneous nerve is more anterior, most commonly passing through the body of coracobrachialis to then run distally in the plane between biceps (superficial) and coracobrachialis (deep).
Highly variable anatomy exists in the axilla with the nerves and vessels, especially with the musculocutaneous nerve which can be adjacent to the median nerve in 10% of cases. Tracing the nerves up from their location in the arm will help with identification in the axilla. Tracing the musculocutaneous nerve more proximally will usually show it moving closer to the axillary artery, eventually becoming adjacent to the median nerve. There are multiple veins in the axilla, usually compressed by probe pressure. Release the probe pressure to see these axillary veins. The deep side of the triangular axillary sheath sits on the fascia covering the conjoint tendon of teres major and latissimus dorsi. The anterior side of the triangular sheath is adjacent to coracobrachialis. The superficial side is adjacent to the deep fascia of the arm.
Practical tips: great care should be taken to avoid IV injection of LA into compressed veins. Aspirate and ensure LA spread in the tissues is observed with every injection. Tourniquet pain (mostly ischaemic muscle pain) is usually adequately covered with axillary blockade despite the cutaneous area of the medial arm not being covered. The medial brachial cutaneous nerve and the intercostobrachial nerve are travelling outside the axillary sheath in a more superficial and posterior location, so will not be blocked with this standard technique. The musculocutaneous nerve is also usually outside the axillary sheath at this level and with lots of anatomical variability may be mis-identified and inadequately blocked. Tracing it proximally and distally is essential for correct identification. Insert the needle in plane from an anterior location that allows all 4 nerves to be accessed and surrounded with LA. If the 4 nerves cannot be confidently identified 20mL of LA around the artery, filling the axillary sheath, will usually block the median, ulnar and radial nerves and be sufficient for hand anaesthesia and analgesia to the arm below the axilla.
A posterior in-plane approach is also possible if the hand is tucked up under the head and the proceduralist is positioned in the axilla (see ergonomics 2 image).
This is the safest brachial plexus block as it avoids any risk of phrenic block or pneumothorax, and any unintended arterial puncture can be easily managed with compression.

notes.full_text:
Interscalene brachial plexus notes
Indications: shoulder anaesthesia and analgesia.
Positioning: lateral, or supine with head turned to contralateral side and pillow behind thoracic spine.
Volume: 7-15 mL.


Side effects: subjective dyspnoea (phrenic nerve block results in 20-30% reduction in respiratory function), hoarse voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve block), Horner’s syndrome (sympathetic chain block). Muscle weakness of shoulder and arm.
Complications: respiratory failure secondary to phrenic nerve block. Brachial plexus root injury. Injury to long thoracic nerve or dorsal scapular nerve (as they pass through the middle scalene muscle), vessel puncture causing haematoma, intravascular injection, intrathecal or epidural injection. Minor paraesthesias for days or weeks are more common with this block than any other block (the nerve roots appear to be very sensitive to injury).


Ultrasound tips: place the probe on the lateral neck over the large vessels at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6). Identify the carotid artery (CA) and the internal jugular vein (IJV). The anterior scalene muscle is the muscle immediately posterior to the CA. The sternocleidomastoid is the most superficial muscle, and its posterior edge usually overlies the middle scalene muscle. The prevertebral fascia usually forms a seagull shape across the top of the scalene muscles, dipping into the interscalene groove. The classic traffic lights pattern of 3 plexus roots in the interscalene groove usually represents C5 and C6 divided, alternatively it may occasionally be C5, C6 and C7. A muscle bridge usually exists between C7 and C8 impairing imaging and LA spread below C7.
Keeping the CA and the IJV on the anterior edge of the image scan caudad and back cephalad looking for the classic traffic light pattern of nerve roots between the scalene muscles. Tilting the probe from transverse to a more caudad direction will help image the structures as they pass laterally towards the shoulder.
Alternatively, the plexus can be traced up from the supraclavicular area where it sits immediately lateral to the subclavian artery (see supraclavicular brachial plexus).
The target for this block is the C5 and C6 plexus roots. It is usually performed around the C7 transverse process level where C5 and C6 run superficially in the interscalene groove.
Cervical levels are confirmed by the shape of the transverse processes. The C7 transverse process is usually deeper than those above and has an absent anterior tubercle which allows imaging of the vertebral artery and vein which are not usually imaged at higher levels. The C6 transverse process is often relatively wide with a prominent anterior tubercle (Chassaignac’s tubercle). (see main menu > Cervical spine > C7&C6 transverse processes).
Look for the dorsal scapular nerve and long thoracic nerve passing through the middle scalene muscle and the common anatomical variation of C5 plexus root passing through or over the anterior scalene muscle.
Use colour doppler as this is a vascular area with vessels and plexus roots both appearing as hypoechoic circles. The transverse cervical artery often traverses this area.
Practical tips: despite the imaging of this area and the block performance being superficial and therefore relatively easy, the plexus roots are very sensitive to damage and there are many important structures in proximity that can be easily injured or inadvertently blocked. To improve safety this block is best performed on awake or lightly sedated patients by experienced clinicians due to the risks of serious complications. Avoid in patients with severe respiratory disease and contralateral phrenic nerve palsy.
The posterior IP approach is the most popular, although anterior and OOP approaches are also used. C8 and T1 plexus roots are usually spared (medial hand, forearm and arm), so choose a lower block of the brachial plexus for surgery below the shoulder. Aim the needle above or between the C5 and C6 plexus roots, do not contact the roots as they are easily damaged, do not pass the needle between the divided C6 plexus roots.
Ensure LA spread is vertical on the screen in the interscalene groove (superficial to deep) rather than a round blob in the middle scalene muscle. It is not necessary to fully surround each plexus root with LA, spread around the posterior surfaces of C5 and C6 is all that is required.
While traditional large volume blocks often spread to the supraclavicular nerves to block the "cape of the shoulder" area, modern US guided low volume blocks do not so these nerves need to be targeted separately to cover this area if required (see Nerves: upper limb > supraclavicular nerves).

Positioning: lateral or supine with head turned to contralateral side and pillow behind thoracic spine.

notes.full_text:
Supraclavicular brachial plexus notes
Indications: anaesthesia to forearm, wrist or hand. Combine with intercostobrachial nerve block for anaesthesia to elbow or for distal humerus surgery. Analgesia to entire arm including shoulder joint.
Positioning: supine with head turned to contralateral side and pillow behind thoracic spine.
Volume: 20-25 mL.
Side effects: Horner’s syndrome (spread to cervical sympathetics), subjective dyspnoea (spread to phrenic nerve), paraesthesiae are common from needle nerve contact. Muscle weakness of arm and hand.
Complications: pneumothorax, artery puncture in non-compressible location, intravascular injection, brachial plexus injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe parallel and cephalad to the mid-clavicle, in the supraclavicular fossa, to identify the subclavian artery. The brachial plexus appears as a “triangular shaped bunch of grapes” immediately lateral to the subclavian artery. The first rib appears as a hyperechoic line with acoustic shadowing deep to it. The pleura is a sliding hyperechoic line deeper on both sides of the rib with lung artifact below. If the probe is angled slightly caudad under the clavicle it is usually possible to image the plexus and subclavian artery on top of the first rib with the pleura deep to the rib. Performing the procedure with this image of the plexus on the rib rather than on the pleura (as it appears slightly more cephalad) reduces the pneumothorax risk. The dorsal scapular artery may be seen passing through the plexus just above this level, check with colour doppler.
Practical tips: this is the easiest part of the brachial plexus to image and provides the most complete block of the arm including everything below the shoulder except for the skin on the medial aspect of the upper arm (intercostobrachial nerve). An in plane lateral to medial approach is the most popular. First inject under the plexus from the lateral extent of the plexus to the angle between the artery and 1st rib (the ‘corner pocket’) to ensure blocking of the inferior trunk. A fascial plane between the trunks/divisions may then sometimes be seen opening from LA spread that may allow safe passage of the needle between trunks/divisions of plexus. Then also spread LA across the superficial edge of the plexus. Occasionally the plexus will extend over the top of the artery to its medial side. Do not inject large volumes superficial and medial to the artery as this will encourage spread to the phrenic nerve.
The suprascapular nerve, (needed for shoulder coverage) may have just left the plexus at this level and may be seen running postero-laterally in the plane under omohyoid. If you are using this block for shoulder analgesia, ensure you identify and do not miss this nerve.
Caution in patients on anticoagulants in view of incompressible location of potential arterial puncture.
Does not cover the intercostobrachial nerve.

notes.full_text:
Infraclavicular brachial plexus (costoclavicular) notes
Indications: anaesthesia to forearm, wrist or hand. Analgesia to entire arm below the shoulder joint. Combine with suprascapular nerve block for shoulder analgesia.
Positioning: supine with head turned to contralateral side and pillow behind thoracic spine. Abducting the arm may elevate the clavicle and improve access to this tight space.
Volume: 15-20 mL.
Side effects: dyspnoea from phrenic block possible. Weakness of arm and hand muscles.
Complications: pneumothorax, vessel puncture in non-compressible location, intravascular injection, brachial plexus injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the transducer transversely, immediately caudad and parallel to the mid clavicle to image the axillary artery. The brachial plexus cords appear immediately lateral to the axillary artery in a triangular wedge shape between subclavius (superficial) and serratus anterior (deep). The plexus appears as 3 discrete cords at this level compared with supraclavicular where divisions often complicate the appearance. The lateral cord is most superficial, medial cord is the deepest and the posterior cord is the most lateral. Tilting the prob cephalad to angle under the clavicle usually helps imaging. Arm abducted to 90º also helps imaging. Deep to serratus anterior is the second rib (hyperechoic line with acoustic shadow deep) and deep to the rib is the pleura (hyperechoic line with sliding movements).
The lateral pectoral nerve may be seen leaving the lateral cord and crossing medially over the axillary artery to then pass superficially to the plane under pectoralis major.
The cephalic vein and the thoracoacromial artery may be seen superficially in this area.
Practical tips: this is a more superficial approach to the brachial plexus below the clavicle than the traditional infraclavicular (coricoid) approach. The cords are more consistently located lateral to the axillary artery and are more compact, so a complete block is more easily achieved. A lateral to medial in plane needle approach is recommended although an out of plane is also possible. Start by injecting around the plexus and look for a fascial plane to open allowing safe needle passage in between the cords.

notes.full_text:
Infraclavicular brachial plexus (coricoid) & (RAPTIR) notes
Indications: anaesthesia to forearm, wrist and hand. Analgesia to entire arm including humerus below the shoulder joint. Combine with suprascapular nerve block for shoulder analgesia.
Positioning: supine with head turned to contralateral side and pillow behind thoracic spine. For the coricoid approach abduct and externally rotate shoulder if possible. For the RAPTIR approach adduct arm and put a support under the shoulder.
Volume: 20-30 mL.
Side effects: muscle weakness of arm and hand.
Complications: pneumothorax, vessel puncture, intravascular injection, brachial plexus injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: a HFL, mid frequency linear or a small curvilinear probe can be used. Place the probe in a sagittal plane just medial to the coracoid process in the deltopectoral groove. Deep to the pectoralis major and minor muscles the axillary artery is seen cephalad to the vein with the lateral, posterior and medial cords around the artery. The cords of the brachial plexus are deep, and difficult to visualise here. The lateral cord is cephalad to the artery and usually easiest seen. The posterior and medial cords start cephalad to the artery in a medial infraclavicular location (as in the costoclavicular approach) and then rotate posteriorly around the artery to end up posterior and caudad to the artery in this coricoid location.
The cephalic vein may be seen superficially or diving deep in the deltopectoral groove to enter the axillary vein. The thoracoacromial artery branches and the lateral pectoral nerve are often seen in close proximity to each other running in the plane between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor.
Practical tips: For the coricoid approach use an IP technique from the cephalad end of the probe. Shoulder abducted to 90º and externally rotated can help imaging. Toeing the probe (heel up) helps needle insertion and needle imaging at the steep insertion angle.
For the RAPTIR approach adduct arm and place a support under the shoulder. Insert the needle a few cm cephalad to the clavicle so the anticipated needle trajectory will be parallel to the probe face and will not impact the clavicle.
The needle tip should be advanced until it lies immediately posterior to the artery. Hydrodisect the lateral and posterior cords away from the needle tip as you advance to this position as they may be in the needle path. Aim to get LA to spread immediately cephalad to the artery and in a U shape immediately posterior to the artery. That is between the artery and the cords. Repositioning the needle is often required for optimal spread. Do not angle medially as the lung is deep and medial.
Phrenic nerve block is extremely unlikely from this location.
This deep block provides a more secure catheter location compared to other more superficial locations of the brachial plexus. This block is difficult in obese patients due to depth.

notes.full_text:
Supraclavicular nerves notes
Indications: cape of shoulder cutaneous anaesthesia and analgesia. Analgesia to clavicle.
Positioning: lateral, or supine with head turned to contralateral side and pillow behind thoracic spine.
Volume: 5-10 mL.
Side effects: subjective dyspnoea possible from phrenic block. Muscle weakness of shoulder and arm from spread to brachial plexus.
Complications: respiratory failure secondary to phrenic nerve block. Brachial plexus root injury. Injury to long thoracic nerve or dorsal scapular nerve, vessel puncture causing haematoma, intravascular injection.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe on the lateral neck over the large vessels at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6). Identify the carotid artery (CA) and the internal jugular vein (IJV). Keeping the CA and the IJV on the anterior edge of the image scan caudad and back cephalad looking for the classic traffic light pattern of nerve roots between the scalene muscles.
The anterior scalene muscle is the muscle immediately posterior to the CA. The sternocleidomastoid is the most superficial muscle, and its posterior edge usually overlies the middle scalene muscle. The prevertebral fascia usually forms a seagull shape across the top of the scalene muscles, dipping into the interscalene groove.
The supraclavicular nerves come from C3 an C4 roots. At the interscalene block level (the traffic lights) usually about C7, the supraclavicular nerve has usually divided and appears as 1-3 small hypoechoic nerves running on the superficial surface of middle scalene in this area. Trace any small hypoechoic nerve like structures seen proximally and the nerves will be seen to join together and enter the interscalene groove a few levels above . Tracing them distally will show them dividing and piercing the superficial cervical fascia to become subcutaneous and continue towards the clavicle. At the C6-7 level the other branches of the superficial cervical plexus have usually become subcutaneous by wrapping around the posterior boarder of sternocleidomastoid and travel in an anterior or cephalad direction. The supraclavicular nerves at this level continue on or over middle scalene in an inferolateral direction.
Use colour doppler as this is a vascular area with vessels and nerve both appearing as hypoechoic circles. The transverse cervical artery often traverses this area.
Practical tips: this block is easily combined with an interscalene or superior trunk block. If the nerves are not seen infiltrating the plane along the superficial boarder of middle scalene at this level will often provide a block.

notes.full_text:
Suprascapular nerve (posterior) notes
Indications: analgesia to posterolateral shoulder. As part of multimodal analgesia for arthroscopic shoulder surgery, or major shoulder surgery when interscalene block is contraindicated due to respiratory compromise. Often combined with other nerve blocks e.g. axillary nerve or infraclavicular brachial plexus for more extensive shoulder analgesia.
Positioning: lateral with operative side uppermost allows for sedation and is usually more comfortable for the patient. Sitting also possible.
Volume: 5-10 mL.
Side effects: weakness of supraspinatus and infraspinatus which provide some external rotation of shoulder.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe parallel and immediately cephalad to the spine of the scapular. Tilt the probe caudad to image the floor of the supraspinous fossa, deep to trapezius and supraspinatus. Slide the probe laterally until the “hockey stick” appearance of the lateral end of the supraspinous fossa appears. The nerve and artery run in a fascial compartment deep to supraspinatus. The artery is only sometimes seen, the nerve rarely seen, but the fascial compartment deep to supraspinatus in the “hockey stick” depression on the bone is easily seen. If the probe is tilted cephalad the suprascapular notch can be imaged as a break in the continuous white line of the supraspinous fossa.
Practical tips: this can be deep in muscular patients impairing imaging. The bone backstop to needle path aids safety. Although the nerve is rarely seen, the fascial compartment under supraspinatus is always seen and the bony backstop makes this a relatively easy and safe block despite the depth. Ensure you have a continuous hyperechoic line of the supraspinous fossa. If you tilt the probe too far cephalad you will see a break in the continuous hyperechoic line which is the scapular notch. Do not perform block with this image of notch as pneumothorax possible. This block is often combined with an axillary nerve block for more extensive shoulder analgesia without any risk of phrenic block. The anterior approach to the suprascapular nerve may provide better analgesia due to LA spreading to the superior trunk (with an accompanying small risk of phrenic block).

notes.full_text:
Suprascapular nerve (anterior) notes
Indications: analgesia of posterolateral shoulder. As part of multimodal analgesia for arthroscopic shoulder surgery, or for major shoulder surgery when interscalene block is not suitable. This block is often combined with other nerve blocks e.g., axillary nerve or supraclavicular brachial plexus for more extensive shoulder analgesia.
Positioning: supine with head turned to contralateral side and pillow behind thoracic spine.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: weakness of supraspinatus and infraspinatus which provide some external rotation of shoulder. However LA often spreads to the upper trunk of the supraclavicular brachial plexus due to its close proximity resulting in more significant shoulder and arm weakness, especially if larger volumes are used.
Complications: vascular puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury, pneumothorax, dyspnoea from phrenic block.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe immediately cephalad and parallel to the mid clavicle to image the subclavian artery and the supraclavicular brachial plexus immediately lateral to the artery. Trace the brachial plexus cephalad to the interscalene groove identifying C5 and C6 roots. Tracing C5 and C6 roots back distally carefully observe the roots dividing into multiple fascicles and combining into a single sheath (the superior trunk). As you carefully trace this superior trunk back to the supraclavicular area look for the most lateral fascicle (the suprascapular nerve) of the superior trunk leaving the superior trunk to travel more laterally away from the rest of the supraclavicular plexus under a long thin muscle (omohyoid) sometimes with a small artery (suprascapular artery). Rotating the lateral end of the probe more posteriorly can sometimes help image this nerve.
Practical tips: if the nerve is not seen, the plane under omohyoid can be infiltrated which will usually block the nerve, or the posterior approach could be used. This anterior approach often provides better analgesia than the posterior approach probably due to LA spreading to the superior trunk. However the anterior approach does come with a risk of phrenic block. If zero risk of phrenic nerve block is desired, choose the posterior approach rather than the anterior approach to this nerve. The posterior approach is often combined with an axillary nerve block for more extensive analgesia with no risk of phrenic block. The anterior approach is easily combined with a superior trunk/ supraclavicular brachial plexus block but does carry a risk of phrenic block.

notes.full_text:
Indications: analgesia to anterior shoulder. Usually combined with a suprascapular nerve block for more extensive shoulder analgesia.
Positioning: lateral with operative side uppermost, elbow flexed and resting in front of patient to internally rotate arm. The lateral position allows sedation and is usually more comfortable for the patient. Sitting also possible.
Volume: 10 mL.
Side effects: deltoid weakness.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: the probe is placed in a sagittal plane over the posterior humeral neck. The posterior circumflex humeral vessels are imaged in short axis coursing around the neck of the humerus. The nerve usually divides into anterior and posterior branches in the quadrangular space just before this location. The anterior branch runs around the posterior humeral neck and innervates the anterior joint capsule. The nerve is often not seen but runs in proximity, (usually cephalad to) the posterior circumflex humeral vessels, deep to deltoid, distal to teres minor insertion and proximal to triceps insertion. The vessels and nerve are sited in a hyperechoic triangular shaped fascial compartment immediately superficial to the bone between the “bow tie” shaped muscle insertions of teres minor (cephalad) and triceps lateral head (caudad). Use colour doppler to identify vessels.
Practical tips: this block is easily added to a posterior suprascapular nerve block for shoulder analgesia without any risk of phrenic nerve block. If the nerve is not seen infiltrate the fascial compartment adjacent to the posterior circumflex humeral artery. The needle can be inserted from the cephalad or caudad end of the probe. Internally rotate the arm and stay as posterior as possible to block the axillary nerve as proximally as possible.

notes.full_text:
Intercostobrachial nerve notes
Indications: anaesthesia to the cutaneous medial aspect of arm and axilla.
Positioning: supine with the arm abducted 90º resting on an arm board or table. Alternatively, with the hand tucked up under the head.
Volume: 10 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: nerve injury, vessel puncture causing haematoma, block failure due to difficulty in directly targeting nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm also innervating this area.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely in the axillary crease to image the axillary vessels. Slide the probe posteriorly placing vessels on the anterior edge of the image. The intercostobrachial nerve has often branched at this level and the branches are not easily identified but usually run superficial to the deep fascia of the arm (fascial plane on the superficial surface of the muscles). Tucking hand behind head and scanning more proximally can sometimes help.
Practical tips: insert the needle in plane from anterior (taking care to avoid the axillary vessels and nerves) to infiltrate the plane superficial to the deep fascia of the arm. Nerves not usually identified. Infiltrate from axillary vessels posteriorly in the plane superficial to the deep fascia. Alternatively, with the hand tucked under head a posterior approach is possible avoiding axillary vessels and nerves. Surround any nerve like structures seen in this plane or more superficially in the subcutaneous fat. Often combined with other brachial plexus blocks (esp. supraclavicular) when incision may involve the medial aspect of the arm. An intercostobrachial nerve block can also be achieved via a high serratus plane block or a pectoserratus plane block however more volume (20mls) will be required.

notes.full_text:
Median nerve mid arm notes
Indications: analgesia to palmar surface of hand or anterior surface of forearm bones. Combine with an ulnar nerve block for palmer surface of hand anaesthesia, or with ulnar and radial nerves for complete hand anaesthesia. Combine with radial nerve block for more complete forearm bone analgesia.
Positioning: supine with the arm abducted to 90º on an arm board or table.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: weakness of hand and wrist flexors.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: trace the brachial artery distally from the axilla down the medial aspect of the arm. The median nerve stays adjacent to the brachial artery while the ulnar nerve moves more posteriorly away from the brachial artery. At the antecubital fossa the median nerve sits medial to the brachial artery.
Practical tips: the nerve is superficial and easily imaged on the medial aspect of the arm. This may be a useful approach if the axilla is not suitable e.g. local infection or too vascular, and the antecubital fossa is not accessible e.g. plaster cast in situ. Usually combined with a radial nerve block on the lateral side of the distal arm for forearm bone analgesia or radial and ulnar nerve blocks for hand anaesthesia. Can be added as a “rescue” block for incomplete brachial plexus block.

notes.full_text:
Ulnar nerve mid arm notes
Indications: anaesthesia to ulnar side of hand (5th finger and metacarpal). Combine with median nerve block for palmar surface of hand anaesthesia. Combine with median and radial nerve blocks for complete hand anaesthesia.
Positioning: supine with the arm abducted to 90º on an arm board or table for anterior approach. Hand tucked under head for posterior approach.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: weakness of finger and thumb adductors.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: trace the brachial artery distally from the axilla down the medial aspect of the arm. The median nerve stays adjacent to the brachial artery. The ulnar nerve leaves the brachial artery to track more posteriorly. It stays superficial and enters the posterior compartment and continues on the superficial aspect of triceps just deep to the deep fascia of the arm. The ulnar nerve is accompanied by a small artery, the superior ulnar collateral artery. The ulnar nerve then tracks posteriorly towards the ulnar groove on the posterior surface of the medial epicondyle at the elbow.
Practical tips: the nerve is superficial and easily imaged on the medial aspect of the mid arm. This may be a useful approach if the axilla is not suitable e.g. local infection or too vascular, and the forearm is not accessible e.g., plaster cast. Usually combined with a median nerve mid arm block and radial nerve distal arm block. Can be used as a “rescue” block for incomplete brachial plexus block. Anterior approach most common when combining with a median nerve block at the same level. Posterior approach also possible by tucking hand up under the head.

notes.full_text:
Radial nerve distal arm notes
Indications: often combined with median and ulnar nerve blocks for hand anaesthesia. Also combined with median nerve block for forearm bone analgesia.
Positioning: Can be performed with elbow flexed 90º and resting on patient’s chest, with a posterior needle approach ( see ergonomics 1 image). Alternatively with arm by side or abducted 90º on arm table, forearm pronated, with an anterior needle approach ( see ergonomics 2 image).
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: weakness of finger and wrist extensors.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely on the mid posterior arm imaging the humerus. Slide the probe distally and laterally to identify the radial nerve leaving the spiral groove of the humerus and running in the lateral intermuscular septum briefly and then between brachialis and brachioradialis more anteriorly together with the radial collateral artery.
Practical tips: this location can be useful if the antecubital fossa is inaccessible due to a forearm plaster. Also useful if an axillary brachial plexus block is performed and identification of the radial nerve in the axilla is difficult or needle access to the radial nerve is difficult due to overlying vessels. Can also be used as a “rescue” block for incomplete brachial plexus block.

notes.full_text:
Medial cutaneous nerve of forearm notes
Indications: cutaneous analgesia to medial forearm.
Positioning: supine with arm abducted 90º on arm table.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the mid medial arm. Identify the basilic vein running superficial to the muscles under the deep fascia, usually just posterior to the brachial vessels. The nerve is small and runs in the same plane and usually near the basilic vein. Trace any nerve like structure proximally and distally to confirm it is a continuous nerve.
Practical tips: this nerve is occasionally missed with axillary brachial plexus blocks as it is a separate nerve in the axilla having branched from the medial cord above the axilla. It usually runs in the axillary sheath between the median and ulnar nerves so will usually be blocked by most axillary techniques. If missed this can be used for “rescue”. Can also be combined with median and radial nerve blocks performed at the antecubital fossa or the mid arm level for medial forearm surgery analgesia.

notes.full_text:
Lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm notes
Indications: cutaneous analgesia to lateral forearm.
Positioning: supine, forearm extended and supinated, arm by side or abducted 90º on arm table.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: nil
Complications: vascular puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely on the anterior mid arm over biceps superficially and brachialis deep. While sliding the probe distally to the antecubital fossa and back up the arm look for a very small flat nerve running in the plane between the two muscles, from medial to lateral as you descend. This is the terminal musculocutaneous nerve. It can also be traced proximally to the axilla. As you trace it distally to the antecubital fossa it wraps around the lateral edge of biceps tendon and pierces the deep fascia of the arm where it can be difficult to see due to being of similar echogenicity to the connective tissue in this area. In the subcutaneous tissues just distal to the ACF it then sits adjacent to the cephalic vein where it is usually much easier to see. It often divides around this level and can sometimes be traced subcutaneously down the lateral forearm.
Practical tips: identify the nerve by tracing down from the biceps/ brachialis plane as described above. Usually blocked near the lateral edge of biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa, however it is often easier to see just proximal to this in the plane between biceps and brachialis or just distal to this when it is in the subcutaneous tissues near the cephalic vein. The nerve starts dividing soon after piercing the deep fascia so blocking it further distally risks missing some branches. Useful block for superficial procedures to the lateral forearm e.g. radiocephalic fistula however surgical infiltration of deeper structures will still be required. Can be combined with median and radial nerve blocks for lateral forearm bone surgery analgesia.

notes.full_text:
Posterior cutaneous nerve of forearm notes
Indications: analgesia to cutaneous posterior forearm and lateral epicondyle.
Positioning: supine with arm by side or abducted 90º on arm table. Forearm pronated. Can also be performed with elbow flexed 90º and resting on patient’s chest.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: vessel puncture, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the posterolateral mid arm and slide probe distally identifying the radial nerve and the radial collateral artery leaving the spiral groove of the humerus into the lateral intermuscular septum and then running anteriorly between brachialis and brachioradialis. The posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm branches from the radial nerve as it leaves the spiral groove or soon after. It stays in the intermuscular septum often with a small artery, as the radial nerve leaves. The nerve runs in this septum between lateral head of triceps posteriorly and brachialis anteriorly for a short distance often dividing into an anterior and posterior division before becoming subcutaneous and dividing further.
Practical tips: block this nerve before it pierces the deep fascia to become subcutaneous as it usually divides into branches at this point and these may be missed if blocked in the subcutaneous tissues. This nerve will be blocked together with the radial nerve if the radial nerve is targeted immediately after it leaves the spiral groove while it is still in the lateral intermuscular septum, or above this point e.g. axillary brachial plexus block. If the radial nerve is blocked distal to where it leaves the lateral intermuscular septum (e.g. between brachialis and brachioradialis in the distal arm or at the ACF over the lateral epicondyle) this nerve will not be blocked and will need to be targeted separately if required.

Median nerve antecubital fossa notes
Indications: analgesia to palmar surface of hand when combined with ulnar nerve block. Combine with radial and ulnar nerve blocks for complete hand anaesthesia. Combine with radial nerve block for analgesia to forearm bones.
Positioning: supine with arm abducted 90º on arm table or arm board, supinated.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: weakness of finger and wrist flexors.

notes.full_text:
Radial nerve antecubital fossa notes
Indications: combine with median and ulnar nerve blocks for complete hand anaesthesia. Combine with median nerve block for analgesia to forearm bones.
Positioning: supine, forearm extended and supinated. Arm by side or abducted 90º on arm table.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side Effects: weakness of forearm and hand extensor muscles.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place transverse probe over lateral side of antecubital fossa to image the cartilage of the humerus capitulum. Usually at this level the radial nerve is elongated in the fascial plane between brachialis medially and brachioradialis laterally. Often the nerve has a spindle shaped “snake eyes” appearance resulting from the nerve about to divide into superficial and deep branches. There is usually a small artery just deep to the radial nerve, the radial collateral artery. Tracing the nerve proximally shows it becoming more rounded and running in the fascial plane between brachialis and brachioradialis and then to the spiral grove of the humerus. Tracing distally shows the nerve dividing into superficial and deep branches in the proximal forearm.
Practical tips: insert the needle IP from the lateral end of the probe. Beware of the small artery often on the deep edge of the nerve that can look like a nerve fascicle. Use colour doppler to confirm this. Blocking the nerve at this level or above, before it divides, blocks both the deep (motor) and superficial (sensory) branches.

notes.full_text:
Radial nerve superficial branch notes
Indications: sensory block to radial nerve distribution of hand.
Positioning: supine, arm by side or abducted 90º on arm table, forearm extended and supinated.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Ultrasound tips: trace the radial nerve distally from the distal arm or antecubital fossa locations. Just distal to the antecubital fossa the radial nerve will be seen to divide into superficial and deep branches. The superficial branch runs in a fascial plane under brachioradialis down the lateral forearm and comes to sit adjacent to the lateral side of the radial artery in the mid forearm before piercing the deep fascia and becoming subcutaneous just proximal to the wrist near the anatomical snuffbox.
Practical tips: this is the sensory branch of the radial nerve with the deep branch providing all the motor innervation. This nerve can be blocked in the plane under brachioradialis in the proximal forearm or traced and blocked further distally. Insert the needle IP from the lateral end of the probe.

notes.full_text:
Ulnar nerve mid forearm notes
Indications: anaesthesia to the 5th metacarpal and digit. Combine with median and radial nerve blocks for anaesthesia of entire hand.
Positioning: supine with arm abducted 90º on arm table or arm board, forearm supinated.
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: weakness of thumb adductors and little finger flexors.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the medial wrist crease to identify the ulnar artery. The ulnar nerve sits on the medial side of the artery. Tracing the nerve and artery proximally up the forearm shows the nerve running adjacent to the artery until about 2/3 of the way up when the artery moves deep and laterally away from the nerve. notes.full_text:
Median nerve mid forearm notes
Indications: combine with ulnar nerve block for anaesthesia to palmer surface of the hand. Usually combined with radial and ulnar blocks for complete hand anaesthesia.
Positioning: supine with forearm extended and supinated. Arm can be by side or abducted 90º on arm table.
Volume: 5 mL.
Complications: nerve injury.
Side effects: weakness of most forearm and hand flexor muscles.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the anterior mid forearm. The median nerve appears in the fascial plane between the superficial and deep flexor digitorum muscles. Tracing the nerve distally shows it to pass very superficially in the carpel tunnel. Tracing the nerve proximally can be difficult just before the antecubital fossa when it dives deep under pronator teres. It then becomes very superficial and is easily imaged on the medial side of the brachial artery in the antecubital fossa.
Rarely a persistent median artery with a bifid median nerve will be seen.
Practical tips: a superficial palmer branch can separate from the nerve about 5-10 cm proximal to the wrist so do not perform the block too distally as this may be missed.

notes.full_text:
Indications: analgesia to hip, femoral shaft and knee. Combine with a sciatic block for more extensive analgesia or for anaesthesia to lower leg and foot.
Positioning: supine. Flatten the bed as much as possible to open any flexing of the hip. Tilt the whole bed head up if the patient requires some head up positioning rather than flexing at hips.
Volume: 10-15 mL.
Side effects: quadriceps weakness.
Complications: vascular puncture causing haematoma, intravascular injection, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe in a transverse orientation in the inguinal crease over the femoral vessels. Identify the femoral vein and artery. Stay as proximal as possible. Nerve imaging difficulty is usually due to scanning too distally as the femoral nerve quickly flattens and divides into multiple branches a few centimetres distal to the inguinal ligament. If the common femoral artery has divided into its deep (profunda) and superficial (subsartorial) branches, imaging is too distal.
Immediately deep and lateral to the artery you will see a large hypoechoic muscle, the iliopsoas. On the superficial surface of the iliopsoas is a bright hyperechoic fascia, the fascia iliaca, that runs medially deep under the artery. The more superficial fascia that runs superficial to the artery is the fascia lata. The femoral nerve is usually seen as a flattened, spindle shaped, hyperechoic, honeycomb structure squashed between the iliopsoas muscle and the fascia iliaca lateral to the artery. Tilting the probe is required to make the nerve and fascia iliaca bright due to anisotropy. The echogenicity of the nerve is usually similar to the fascia iliaca making it difficult to distinguish the superficial margin of the nerve from the fascia iliaca. The hypoechoic fascicles in the nerve are the most distinguishing feature. LA injected in the plane just below the fascia iliaca hydrodisects the nerve from the fascia iliaca making imaging the nerve much easier.
The superficial circumflex iliac artery may occasionally be seen branching from the femoral artery and running laterally as a linear hypoechoic structure between the fascia iliaca and the more superficial fascia lata.
Practical tips: in obese patients an assistant will be required to retract the abdominal pannus so the probe can image proximally enough in the inguinal crease. Advance the needle from the lateral end of the probe to penetrate the fascia iliaca at the lateral edge of the nerve. Use colour doppler to exclude the deep circumflex iliac artery being in your needle path. LA can be placed above and/or below the nerve but must be deep to the fascia iliaca. Ensure your LA is spreading under the fascial plane that runs under the artery, not above it. The LA often tracts between branches of the nerve giving the appearance of the nerve separating into segments.
If the nerve is not confidently seen, placing LA deep to the fascia iliaca lateral to the artery will usually achieve a block.

notes.full_text:
Sciatic nerve (popliteal fossa) notes
Indications: anaesthesia and analgesia to foot, ankle and leg. Covers most structures below the knee except those innervated by the saphenous nerve and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh. Combine with a saphenous nerve block (usually via an adductor canal block) for anaesthesia to foot, ankle and distal leg.
Positioning: lateral is most ergonomic but can be performed supine or prone.
Volume: 20 mL.
Side effects: weakness of ankle flexors and extensors and intrinsic muscles of the foot.
Complications: nerve injury, vessel puncture causing haematoma, LAST.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely in the popliteal fossa. Identify the popliteal vessels first (the vein is usually superficial to the artery) then the tibial nerve immediately superficial to the vessels. Trace the tibial nerve proximally to identify the smaller common peroneal nerve coming from superficial and lateral to join the tibial nerve, together forming the sciatic nerve usually about 10 cm above the popliteal crease. Firm probe pressure helps imaging. The nerves are highly anisotropic and require tilting of the probe to image nerve margins clearly. The common peroneal nerve often appears to contain a single large (hypoechoic) fascicle. Flexing and extending the ankle, when possible, makes the nerves “seesaw” against each other aiding identification.
Practical tips: This block is usually performed where the two nerves are first enclosed in a common perineural sheath. If this junction is too deep and imaging poor (due to obesity) the nerves can be blocked more distally where they are more superficial and easily imaged as two separate nerves. Small branches to the sural nerve may be seen coming from both nerves and may be missed if the block is performed too distally. Placing the needle tip inside the common perineural sheath (but outside the epineurium surrounding each nerve) where it appears stretching between the two nerves as they come together is a common technique. This provides a faster onset, more reliable block as the thick perineural sheath otherwise slows LA diffusion to the nerves. Good imaging, needle control and injection technique is required to achieve this safely and avoid intraneural injection.
The not covered saphenous nerve innervation is to the skin on the medial leg including over the medial malleolus and sometimes distally to level of 1st metatarsal head, and to some periosteum of the medial malleolus and medial ankle joint. The not covered posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh occasionally extends to innervate some cutaneous area on the posterior proximal leg.

notes.full_text:
Adductor canal (saphenous nerve) notes
Indications: combined with a popliteal sciatic block to complete lower leg, ankle and foot anaesthesia. Popular block for TKR analgesia, when it is often combined with an iPACK block.
Positioning: supine with hip and knee slightly flexed and externally rotated.
Volume: 5-10 mL.
Side effects: quadriceps weakness possible if LA spreads proximally to motor branches of the femoral nerve.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, intravascular injection, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the medial aspect of the mid-thigh. Slide the probe more posteriorly and back anteriorly to identify the sartorius as the most superficial, most hyperechoic, boat shaped muscle on the medial mid-thigh with the femoral artery immediately deep to it. Then slide the probe distally from mid-thigh towards the distal third keeping the femoral artery under sartorius centered on your image. The target is the area just distal to mid thigh, immediately anterior to the artery, deep to the vasoadductor membrane (bright fascial plane between sartorius and artery, extending from the lateral edge of adductor magnus to the medial edge of vastus medialis). The saphenous nerve is immediately anterior to the artery but is only sometimes able to be visualised before LA injection. Usually more easily imaged after LA injection.
Practical tips: pass the needle in plane from the anterior end of the probe. Release probe pressure to see the femoral vein usually just deep to the artery. Ensure LA spreads deep to the vasoadductor membrane, anterior to the artery, not in the more superficial plane between sartorius and the vasoadductor membrane. If you slide too distally towards the distal thigh the saphenous nerve may have crossed over the top of the artery to sit on its posterior side towards the distal end of the adductor canal. The adductor canal block targets the saphenous nerve and is usually used in combination with a popliteal sciatic nerve block to complete anaesthesia or analgesia below the knee. It is also often combined with an iPACK block for TKR analgesia.
The nerve to vastus medialis (which provides more extensive anteromedial joint analgesia for TKR) is not usually blocked with this technique as it has usually divided into branches and runs in a separate fascial tunnel in or on vastus medialis at this level distal to mid thigh. To achieve block of the nerve to vastus medialis as well as the saphenous nerve for TKR perform this block at or just proximal to mid thigh level, or see the slightly more proximal “Femoral triangle distal” block.

notes.full_text:
Lumbar plexus (shamrock) notes
Indications: hip analgesia. Combined with sacral plexus for whole lower limb analgesia. (lumbar plexus includes: femoral, obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous, genitofemoral, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves).
Positioning: lateral.
Volume: 20 mL.
Side effects: quadriceps and adductor muscles weakness.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma in an incompressible location (psoas is a very vascular muscle), lumbar arteries also in this area, intravascular injection, LAST, plexus injury, epidural spread, total spinal if injection into a dural cuff, renal or intraperitoneal puncture.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe transversely on the lateral abdomen between iliac crest and costal margin, in the mid-axillary line. Ensure the depth is set adequately to image vertebrae ( at least 10 cm). Slide the probe slightly posteriorly and rock the probe very slightly in the anterior-posterior plane to image the vertebrae. Once a vertebra is imaged slide the probe slightly in a cephalad-caudad direction to image a transverse process. Next adjust the depth to place the vertebrae towards the bottom of your screen to optimise imaging of muscles above the transverse process.
The quadratus lumborum is usually an inverted triangular shaped muscle that appears more hypoechoic (darker) than the other muscles. Its deep apex inserts onto the transverse process. Superficial and anterior to it will be thin abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominus). Superficial and posterior will be latissimus dorsi. Deep and anterior to quadratus is psoas major, which is usually more hyperechoic than the other muscles, and is immediately adjacent to the vertebral body and anterior surface of the transverse process. Deep and posterior to quadratus is the erector spinae which adjoins the posterior boarder of the transverse process. The “Shamrock sign” is the three-leaf clover appearance of the psoas, quadratus and erector spinae (the leaves) around the transverse process (the stem). The lumbar plexus is not easily seen but usually appears hyperechoic and lies in the posterior third of the psoas.
Practical tips: to allow needle passage from posterior, slide the probe slightly cephalad or caudad to move off the transverse process and image a space between transverse processes (see sonoanatomy 2 above). This will allow needle passage from posterior, between transverse processes to access the posterior psoas and lumbar plexus location.
Consider LA with adrenalin as very vascular muscle.
Not often indicated due to depth, imaging difficulty, high incidence of complications and availability of safer more distal alternatives. Nerve stimulation recommended in addition to ultrasound as plexus not usually seen clearly due to depth.

Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe transversely on the lateral abdomen between iliac crest and costal margin, in the mid-axillary line. Ensure the depth is set adequately to image vertebrae ( at least 10 cm). Slide the probe slightly posteriorly and rock the probe very slightly in the anterior-posterior plane to image the vertebrae. Once a vertebra is imaged slide the probe slightly in a cephalad-caudad direction to image a transverse process. Next adjust the depth to place the vertebrae towards the bottom of your screen to optimise imaging of muscles above the transverse process.
The quadratus lumborum is usually an inverted triangular shaped muscle that appears more hypoechoic (darker) than the other muscles. Its deep apex inserts onto the transverse process. Superficial and anterior to it will be thin abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominus). Superficial and posterior will be latissimus dorsi. Deep and anterior to quadratus is psoas major, which is usually more hyperechoic than the other muscles, and is immediately adjacent to the vertebral body and anterior surface of the transverse process. Deep and posterior to quadratus is the erector spinae which adjoins the posterior boarder of the transverse process. The “Shamrock sign” is the three-leaf clover appearance of the psoas, quadratus and erector spinae (the leaves) around the transverse process (the stem). The lumbar plexus is not easily seen but usually appears hyperechoic and lies in the posterior third of the psoas.
notes.practical_tips:
to allow needle passage from posterior, slide the probe slightly cephalad or caudad to move off the transverse process and image a space between transverse processes (see sonoanatomy 2 above). This will allow needle passage from posterior, between transverse processes to access the posterior psoas and lumbar plexus location.
Consider LA with adrenalin as very vascular muscle.
Not often indicated due to depth, imaging difficulty, high incidence of complications and availability of safer more distal alternatives. Nerve stimulation recommended in addition to ultrasound as plexus not usually seen clearly due to depth.

notes.full_text:
Lumbar plexus (trident) notes
Indications: hip analgesia. Combined with sacral plexus for whole lower limb analgesia. (lumbar plexus includes: femoral, obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous, genitofemoral, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves).
Positioning: lateral.
Volume: 20mL.
Side effects: quadriceps and adductor muscles weakness.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma in an incompressible location (psoas is a very vascular muscle), lumbar arteries also in this area, intravascular injection, LAST, plexus injury, epidural spread, total spinal if injection into a dural cuff, renal or intraperitoneal puncture.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe in a sagittal, paramedian orientation over the mid lumbar spine level. Slide the probe laterally until transverse process tips disappear, then back medially until they reappear. Usually, three transverse processes fit onto the screen and their acoustic shadows form a “trident” appearance. Superficial to the transverse processes will be the erector spinae muscles, deep to the transverse processes will be the psoas muscle. Deep to the psoas the kidney or peritoneal cavity may be imaged. The plexus is not usually seen but is located in the posterior third of the psoas and may appear as a hyperechoic linear structure.
Practical tips: not indicated often due to depth, imaging difficulty, high incidence of complications and availability of safer more distal alternatives. Nerve stimulation recommended as plexus not usually seen due to depth, and needle imaging is difficult due to the steep angle of insertion. The Shamrock approach (see Lumbar plexus shamrock) to the lumbar plexus is more popular due to familiarity with imaging (for quadratus lumborum blocks) and the needle angle being more parallel to the probe face aiding imaging.
Consider LA with adrenalin as psoas is a very vascular muscle.

notes.full_text:
Indications: combined with a lumbar plexus block can provide anaesthesia to entire lower limb if a neuraxial is not possible. A proximal approach to the sciatic nerve if more distal approaches are not possible. For anaesthesia of the leg below the knee when combined with saphenous nerve block. Analgesia to posterior hip and thigh.
Positioning: lateral with hips flexed.
Volume: 20 mL.
Side effects: weakness of hip stabilizers, hamstrings, calf and foot muscles.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma in deep incompressible location, intravascular injection, LAST, plexus injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe on the medial half of a line connecting PSIS to greater trochanter. Image the gluteus maximus muscle superficially with the gluteus medius deep to it and the continuous hyperechoic line of the ilium deep to gluteus medius. Slide the probe sideways, in an inferomedial direction towards the natal cleft (parallel shift) a few cm until a break in the continuous bony contour of the ilium is seen. This is the sacral hiatus. Slide slightly further until the lateral side of this hiatus is formed by the posterior border of the ischium which has a characteristic curved shape on ultrasound and is the main landmark. The triangular shaped piriformis muscle will also be seen at this level covering this space from its origin deep to the medial sacral bone and extending laterally superficial to the ishium. Tilt the probe slightly caudally to image the sacral plexus as a hyperechoic structure, deep to piriformis in the sacral hiatus. The inferior gluteal artery is usually seen at the medial end of the plexus. Use colour doppler.
Practical tips: insert the needle from the lateral end of the probe. This block can be difficult in many patients due to depth. Rarely indicated as neuraxial blocks or easier and safer more distal sciatic blocks are usually available.

notes.full_text:
Fascia iliaca (suprainguinal) notes
Indications: analgesia to hip, femur, anterior and lateral thigh. Popular analgesia for patients with a fractured neck of femur.
Positioning: supine. Flatten the bed as much as possible to open any flexing of the hip. Tilt the whole bed head up if the patient requires some head up positioning rather than flexing at the hip.
Volume: 20-40 mL.
Side effects: quadriceps weakness.
Complications: LAST, nerve injury, vessel puncture causing haematoma in deep pelvic location, peritoneal cavity puncture.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe over the ASIS in a sagittal orientation. Slide the probe inferomedially along the inguinal ligament towards the pubic symphysis following the bony contour of the ilium. After only 1-2cm the AIIS should be seen as a peaked hyperechoic shape. Sometimes the AIIS is not that peaked or that different from the adjacent pelvic brim. Overlying this bony landmark is the large iliacus muscle with the internal oblique muscle superficial and cephalad and the sartorius superficial and caudad, together making a superficial “bow-tie” appearance. The fascia iliaca is the hyperechoic fascial layer covering the superficial surface of the iliacus muscle. The deep circumflex iliac vessels are usually seen superficial to the fascia iliaca in the pelvis. Use colour doppler to help identify these. The peritoneum is also superficial to the fascia iliaca a few cm further cephalad.
Practical tips: this block targets the femoral nerve including its high pelvic branches, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. Coverage of the obturator nerve is controversial and would appear unreliable at best. Compared with the infrainguinal technique this suprainguinal technique is theoretically more likely to block the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (as the site of injection is closer to this nerve) and some higher branches of the femoral nerve that innervate the hip joint. Insert the needle from the caudad end of the probe. Align the needle trajectory with the intrapelvic fascia iliaca. Tent and pop through the fascia iliaca and then withdraw the needle tip slightly until just deep to the fascia iliaca.The injected LA should be seen opening ("unzipping") the plane between the fascia iliaca and the iliacus muscle (not separating fibres within the iliacus muscle). The LA should be seen spreading cephalad in this fascia iliaca plane deep to the deep circumflex iliac vessels into the pelvis.  Keep the needle tip in view and deep to the fascia iliaca in the pelvis to avoid puncture of the deep circumflex iliac vessels and the peritoneum.

notes.full_text:
Fascia iliaca (infrainguinal) notes
Indications: analgesia to hip, femur, anterior and lateral thigh. Popular analgesia for patients with a fractured neck of the femur.
Positioning: supine. Flatten the bed as much as possible to open any flexing of the hip. Tilt the whole bed head up if the patient requires some head up positioning rather than flexing at the hip.
Volume: 30-40 mL.
Side effects: quadriceps weakness.
Complications: LAST, nerve injury, vessel puncture causing haematoma.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely in the femoral crease over the large vessels. Identify the femoral artery with the vein medial to it. Stay as proximal as possible over the inguinal crease. Ensure you are proximal enough that the common femoral artery has not yet divided into its deep (profunda) and its superficial (subsartorial) branches. Lateral and deep to the artery a large hypoechoic muscle will be seen with its superficial boarder extending deep to the artery. This is the iliopsoas muscle. The hyperechoic superficial surface of this muscle is the fascia iliaca. The fascia iliaca extends deep to the artery. A more superficial fascia that extends superficial to the artery is the fascia lata. Tilting the probe will make these fascial planes easier to see. You may see the femoral nerve as an elongated, spindle shaped hyperechoic structure with internal hypoechoic fascicles, lateral to the artery, squashed between the iliopsoas muscle and the fascia iliaca. The nerve often appearing to blend into the fascia iliaca. The target plane is between the iliopsoas muscle and the fascia iliaca, lateral to the neurovascular bundle and as proximal as possible but distal to the inguinal ligament.
Practical tips: this block targets the femoral nerve and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve by injecting a large volume of LA in the plane under the fascia iliaca that both nerves traverse and expecting the LA to spread to both nerves. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve traverses this plane above the inguinal ligament hence a large volume and proximal injection site is required to get spread to it. This technique does not block the obturator nerve.
Below the inguinal ligament, with ultrasound, there is little reason to perform this fascia iliaca fascial plane block if you can more directly target the femoral nerve and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve as two specific nerve blocks.
If the indication is for pre-op analgesia for a fractured neck of femur, the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block contributes nothing to pre op analgesia so a targeted femoral nerve block will be more specific and achieved with less volume. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block will provide additional analgesia for a lateral surgical incision when the patient comes to theatre.
A suprainguinal fascia iliaca block has also been described which should be more effective as it is closer to the LFCN and more proximal branches of the femoral nerve, but is slightly more difficult with greater risks. It is however recommended over this approach. See Fascia iliaca (suprainguinal).
