notes.full_text:
Pericapsular nerve group (PENG) notes
Indications: analgesia to anterior hip joint capsule.
Positioning: supine with no hip flexion. Flatten the bed as much as possible. Tilt the whole bed head up if the patient requires some head up positioning rather than flexing at the hip.
Volume:10-20 mL.
Side effects: usually nil. Quadriceps weakness is possible if LA spreads to the femoral nerve.
Complications: vessel puncture, femoral nerve injury, ureter injury, joint capsule puncture, LFCN injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the ASIS. Slide caudally and medially a few cm along the ilium to image the AIIS as the next peaking bony contour. Rotate the medial end of the probe 45 degrees to point towards the pubis and tilt caudally to image the ilium from AIIS to iliopubic eminence (IPE) as a continuous hyperechoic line. The dip between the AIIS and the IPE is the iliopsoas notch. Identify the femoral vessels and femoral nerve superficially. The psoas tendon is often seen as a hyperechoic area deep in the psoas muscle above the iliopsoas notch. The target plane is deep to psoas and psoas tendon, and immediately superficial to the bone of the iliopsoas notch between AIIS and IPE. If the femoral head or joint space is imaged, you are too distal and need to slide the probe proximally to image ilium with AIIS, iliopsoas notch and IPE as a continuous hyperechoic line. If you slide too far cephalad the bony contour disappears deep into the pelvis.
Practical tips: this is a motor sparing block of the anterior hip capsule nerves ( sensory branches of the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves). Insert the needle from the lateral end of the probe. Navigate over AIIS and then advance to hit the ilium bone in the iliopsoas notch. The target plane is between the psoas muscle / tendon and bone. LA should be seen lifting the psoas tendon / muscle from the ilium and spreading in the plane deep to the muscle and tendon, immediately superficial to the bone. If you inject into the muscle or the fascial plane between iliacus and psoas you will increase the risk of LA spread to the femoral nerve. A curvilinear probe is usually required. Toeing the probe helps with needle imaging for the steep insertion angle. Ensure you have a continuous hyperechoic bony contour as your target. Too cephalad will put you into the pelvis, too caudad will put you into the hip joint capsule. This block is easily combined with a LFCN block for lateral incisions. A high frequency linear probe is required for the LFCN block due it being a small, superficial nerve. See Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

notes.full_text:
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve notes
Indications: anaesthesia and analgesia to the skin on the lateral thigh distal to the greater trochanter level.
Positioning: supine and flat (without hip flexion, to allow access to groin crease).
Volume: 5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely in the inguinal crease over the large vessels to image the femoral artery, vein and nerve. The first muscle deep and lateral to the artery is the iliopsoas with the fascia iliaca on its superficial surface. Slide the probe further laterally and the next muscle superficial and lateral to iliopsoas is sartorius, with rectus femoris deep to it. Sartorius is usually more hyperechoic than the other muscles and is the most superficial of all the muscles. Keep sliding the probe laterally to focus on the lateral border of sartorius.
Lateral to sartorius there is usually a small, fat filled, inverted triangular fascial compartment before tensor fascia lata, the next further lateral muscle. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is usually seen in this fascial compartment on the lateral side of sartorius. The nerve is small, hyperechoic with small fascicles. Scanning proximally and distally over this compartment, tracing the nerve, is required to reliably identify the nerve. Proximally the nerve will usually pass medially over the superficial boarder of sartorius with a flatter shape and similar echogenicity to the connective tissue which makes it difficult to trace in the fascial tissues. Distally in the fat filled compartment the nerve is often seen to divide into branches and has a rounder appearance that is easier to identify with the contrast of the surrounding hypoechoic fat. The nerve branches can often be traced down the lateral thigh.
Practical tips: this block is easily combined with a femoral nerve block or a PENG block. Sensory innervation is usually over the lateral thigh distal to the greater trochanter level. Surgical incisions extending proximal to the greater trochanter will therefore need some proximal wound infiltration or cluneal/ subcostal nerve block for analgesia. If you are unable to identify the nerve, the fascial plane superficial to sartorius just distal to ASIS can be infiltrated as the nerve usually runs here. Block the nerve as proximally as possible before it divides into branches.

notes.full_text:
Obturator nerve (subpectineal) notes
Indications: analgesia to medial thigh, femur and knee. Often combined with femoral or fascia iliaca blocks for more extensive analgesia. Can be used for motor block of adductor muscles for lateral bladder wall diathermy procedures.
Positioning: supine with leg slightly abducted and externally rotated.
Volume: 10-15 mL.
Side effects: adductor muscle weakness.
Complications: nerve injury, vascular puncture causing haematoma in an incompressible location, LAST as often combined with other blocks.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely in the inguinal crease over the large vessels. Identify the femoral artery and vein. Slide the probe medially, identifying pectineus which is the muscle immediately deep and medial to the vein. Keep sliding medially to identify the next 3 muscle layers immediately medial to pectineus. These are adductor longus most superficial, adductor brevis and adductor magnus the deepest. With pectineus in the image slide as cephalad as possible and the tilt probe further cephalad to image the superior pubic ramus and the fascial plane deep to pectineus. The muscle deep to pectineus is the obturator externus. The target plane is between pectineus and obturator externus. Sometimes the obturator vessels and nerves will be seen in this plane.
Practical tips: ensure bed is flat (no hip flexion) to allow optimal access to groin. Easily combined with a femoral nerve block or adductor canal block for more complete knee analgesia. Pass the needle in plane from the lateral end of the probe. Nerve not often seen. The aim is to infiltrate the fascial plane deep to pectineus that the nerve runs through. Beware of obturator vessels that also run in this plane and may be incompressible in this location if punctured. Use colour doppler to help identify these.

notes.full_text:
Obturator nerve branches notes
Indications: analgesia to medial thigh, femur and knee. Often combined with femoral or fascia iliaca blocks for more extensive analgesia. Can also be used for motor block of adductor muscles for lateral bladder wall diathermy procedures.
Positioning: supine with leg slightly abducted and externally rotated.
Volume: 7- 10 mL per nerve.
Side effects: adductor muscles weakness.
Complications: nerve injury, vascular puncture causing haematoma, LAST as often combined with other blocks.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely in the inguinal crease over the large vessels. Identify the femoral artery and vein. Deep and lateral to the artery is iliopsoas. Slide the probe medially, identifying pectineus which is the muscle deep and medial to the vein. Keep sliding medially to identify the next 3 muscle layers immediately medial to pectineus. These are adductor longus most superficial, adductor brevis and adductor magnus the deepest.
The anterior and posterior branches of the obturator nerve can usually be seen as hyperechoic flattened nerves running in the planes between the adductor muscles. The anterior branch runs between adductor longus and brevis. The posterior branch runs between adductor brevis and magnus. Tracing these nerves proximally shows them travelling anterolaterally in these planes to join in the plane under pectineus. Tracing distally, they run posteromedially in these planes. There are often small branches of the obturator vessels also running in these planes with the nerves. Use colour doppler to help identify these vessels.
Practical tips: ensure the bed is flat (no hip flexion) with some abduction and external rotation to allow optimal access to proximal medial groin. This can be a deep and difficult block in obese patients and pannus retraction is often required. Easily combined with a femoral nerve block.
Pass the needle in plane from the anterolateral end of the probe. Commonly the block is performed where the anterior branch is at the pectineus/adductor longus/adductor brevis junction and the posterior branch is in the plane between adductor brevis and adductor magnus. If the nerves are not seen the fascial planes can be infiltrated which will usually achieve a block and the nerves will often become more visible. The posterior branch is the branch that contributes to knee innervation so can be selectively blocked if knee analgesia is the indication.

notes.full_text:
Sciatic nerve (anterior) notes
Indications: when other approaches to the sciatic nerve are not possible.
Positioning: leg slightly abducted and externally rotated to give access to upper medial thigh.
Volume: 15-20 mL.
Side effects: weakness of hamstrings, ankle plantar flexors and dorsiflexors, intrinsic foot muscles.
Complications: nerve injury, vascular puncture in deep location, LAST when combined with other blocks.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe transversely on the anteromedial aspect of the upper thigh. Adjust the depth so the femur appears around the middle of the screen. Identify the superficial and deep femoral vessels in a fascial plane extending down to the femur. On the medial side of this fascial plane is the medial muscle group consisting of the 3 adductor muscles. The sciatic nerve is usually seen just deep and medial to the femur in the fascial plane deep to the adductor muscles and anterior to the posterior muscle group. It appears flattened, hyperechoic and very anisotropic. If the probe is too anterolateral the nerve may be hidden behind the femur. Slide the probe more medially.
Practical tips: difficult block due to depth. Posterior approaches are easier, but this is an option if the patient cannot be rolled laterally, or the leg lifted to give access to the posterior thigh. Needle approach from the medial end of probe is usually safer as it avoids the femoral vessels. Out of plane approach could also be used. Consider the use of a nerve stimulator to confirm the nerve if pathology allows.

notes.full_text:
Sciatic nerve (transgluteal) notes
Indications: analgesia to knee, leg, ankle and foot. Combined with a saphenous nerve block (via femoral nerve block or adductor canal block) for anaesthesia to foot, ankle and distal leg.
Positioning: lateral.
Volume:15-20 mL.
Side effects: weakness of knee flexors, ankle flexors and extensors, and intrinsic muscles of foot.
Complications: nerve injury, vascular puncture in deep location, LAST especially when combined with other blocks.
Ultrasound tips: place a curvilinear probe midway along a line between the greater trochanter and sacral hiatus. Identify gluteus maximus superficially, greater trochanter laterally, ischium medially, quadratus femoris deep. The sciatic nerve is usually a flattened hyperechoic structure in the fascial plane joining these two bony landmarks, deep to gluteus maximus, superficial to quadratus femoris. The nerve can be difficult to see due to depth, anisotropy and sometimes a very flattened nerve in the fascial plane. A small artery sometimes accompanies the nerve.
Practical tips: rarely used as more distal blocks are usually preferred. High approaches to the sciatic nerve can be useful when popliteal fossa access not possible eg long leg cast, however infragluteal sciatic nerve approach is usually much easier and preferred to this approach. Nerve stimulation can be helpful in confirming nerve location. An in plane needle approach from the lateral side is usually chosen.

notes.full_text:
Femoral triangle apex notes
Indications: blocks the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis. Usually used for motor sparing knee analgesia following TKR.
Positioning: supine. Leg slightly abducted and externally rotated.
Volume: 10 mL.
Side effects: vastus medialis weakness.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, intravascular injection, LAST if combined with other blocks, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the medial aspect of the mid-thigh. Slide the probe more postero-medially and back antero-laterally to identify the sartorius as the most superficial, most hyperechoic, boat shaped muscle on the medial mid-thigh with the femoral artery immediately deep to it. Sliding the probe from distal to proximal along the medial border of sartorius, identify the adductor longus which will appear as a small muscle under the medial side of sartorius and getting much larger as it is traced proximally. Trace adductor longus back distally and it will get smaller disappearing under sartorius to insert into the femur. Trace adductor longus back proximally to identify where the medial border of adductor longus crosses the medial border of sartorius. This point marks the apex of the femoral triangle and the start of the adductor canal. The vasoadductor membrane ( thick fascial plane joining the lateral side of adductor magnus to the medial side of vastus medialis, passing between sartorius and the femoral artery), appears distal to this level forming a "roof" to the true adductor canal.
Perform the block just proximal to this femoral triangle apex level. Release probe pressure to identify the femoral vein usually deep to the artery. The saphenous nerve is always lateral to the artery at this level and may be seen as a small hyperechoic nerve especially after LA has been injected. The nerve to vastus medialis is less often seen but is usually slightly more lateral to the saphenous nerve in the plane between sartorius and vastus medialis.
Practical tips: the femoral triangle apex block targets the saphenous nerve as well as the nerve to vastus medialis. This provides more extensive medial knee analgesia than just a saphenous nerve block in the adductor canal. 10 mL is usually adequate as larger volumes may result in spread to more proximal femoral nerve branches and can result in more motor weakness. If the apex of the femoral triangle cannot be accurately identified with US as described above perform the block midway between ASIS and proximal patella. If only a saphenous nerve block is desired (eg to combine with a popliteal sciatic block for lower leg anaesthesia or analgesia), perform the block more distal to this level in the mid adductor canal. See Adductor canal (saphenous nerve).

notes.full_text:
iPACK = infiltration between popliteal artery and capsule of the knee.
Indications: analgesia to the posterior capsule of the knee. Often combined with an adductor canal block or femoral triangle apex block for more extensive motor sparing analgesia for TKR.
Positioning: Supine with hip flexed and externally rotated, knee slightly flexed (frog leg position). This position is commonly used after femoral triangle apex/adductor canal block performed. Lateral often easier imaging and can be done after spinal and before going supine for femoral triangle apex/adductor canal block.
Volume: 10-20 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: vascular puncture causing haematoma, LA spread to tibial and common peroneal nerves can result in motor weakness of leg muscles causing foot drop, LAST when combined with other blocks.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe over the posterior aspect of the distal thigh just above the level of the proximal patella. Identify the femur and the popliteal artery. The tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve may be seen posterior and superficial to the vessels. The target plane is between the artery and the femur.
Practical tips: In the supine frog leg position, slide the probe more posteriorly into a postero-medial location so the needle trajectory will be parallel to the posterior surface of the femur. Insert the needle from the medial end of the probe, advancing between femur and popliteal artery until just lateral to the artery. Inject a few mL here and the remainder while withdrawing to infiltrate the plane between the artery and the femur. This block is easily combined with an adductor canal block or femoral triangle apex block for TKR.

iPACK (lateral) notes
iPACK = infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee.
Indications: analgesia to the posterior capsule of the knee. Often combined with an adductor canal block or femoral triangle apex block for more extensive motor sparing analgesia for TKR.

This block is easily combined with an adductor canal block or femoral triangle apex block for TKR analgesia.

notes.full_text:
Superior medial geniculate nerves notes
Indications: analgesia to anterior knee joint.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 3-5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: vessel puncture, intravascular injection, LAST as often combined with other blocks, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the HFL probe in a longitudinal plane over the antero-medial distal femur. Image the femoral shaft and the vastus medialis muscle above. Then slide the probe distally until the metaphysis of the femur is seen ( where the shaft starts to slope superficially towards the medial epicondyle). This is usually at the level of the superior pole of the patella. Hold the probe still and look for the small pulsing movements of the SMGA in short axis coursing around the femoral metaphysis, deep to vastus medialis. Colour doppler can help. The SMGN is usually not seen but runs in the same plane, deep to the muscle, near the SMGA.

notes.full_text:
Tibial nerve (ankle) notes
Indications: anaesthesia and analgesia to the sole of the foot. Useful for removal of foreign body. Often combined with other nerves for an ankle block of the entire foot.
Positioning: usually supine with the leg externally rotated and knee flexed into a figure 4 position. Alternatively, lateral with medial malleolus uppermost, or supine with leg elevated by supports under calf allowing access for a posterior needle insertion. Prone also possible.
Volume: 5-8 mL.
Side effects: weakness of intrinsic foot muscles.
Complications: nerve injury, vascular puncture.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe proximal to the medial malleolus between the tibia and the achilles tendon. Identify the posterior tibial artery and veins. The tibial nerve usually lies posterior to the vessels lying on flexor hallucis longus muscle. The flexor hallucis longus tendon within the muscle should not be confused with the nerve. Trace these structures proximally and distally to confirm their identity.
Practical tips: usually performed as part of an ankle block. Block this nerve first as it is the largest, has the slowest onset, and is usually the most important. A needle insertion from the posterior end of the probe provides the best needle trajectory because of the vessels anterior to the nerve. An OOP approach has easier ergonomics. Use smaller gauge needles for patient comfort if performing awake.

notes.full_text:
Deep peroneal nerve notes
Indications: analgesia to the area between great and second toes and much of the deeper structures on the dorsal aspect of the foot. Usually combined with other nerve blocks to achieve ankle block of entire foot.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 2-5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: nerve injury, vessel puncture.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the anterior ankle joint. Slide slightly proximally to image the distal tibia rather than the joint space. Identify the anterior tibial artery, usually with one or two veins, sitting close to the distal tibia. Use very light probe pressure to avoid compressing these vessels. Trace the artery proximally and back distally to identify the deep peroneal nerve as a small group of hypoechoic circles (fascicles) or string of fascicles passing over the artery from lateral to medial as it descends. The nerve can often be traced 5-10cm more proximal where it enters the anterior compartment of the leg and travels proximally on the interosseous membrane.
Practical tips: release the probe pressure or consider using a tourniquet to see the veins. Use a smaller gauge needle for patient comfort, and ease of penetrating skin and fascial planes. Pass the needle in plane from medial or lateral depending on position of the nerve relative to the artery. An out of plane approach is also often chosen for this very superficial block.

notes.full_text:
Superficial peroneal nerve notes
Indications: analgesia to much of the dorsal surface of the foot. Usually combined with other nerve blocks to achieve ankle block of the entire foot.
Positioning: lateral, operative side uppermost. Supine with foot elevated on support also possible.
Volume: 3-5 mL.
Side effects: nil (as block is usually performed distal to motor branches to peroneal muscles but a foot drop is possible if motor supply to peroneus longus and brevis is blocked).
Complications: nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely on the lateral aspect of the mid fibula. Scan from proximal 1/3 to distal 1/3 looking for the peaking of the bony contour of the fibular pointing superficially to the fascial plane (anterior intermuscular septum) between the lateral compartment (peroneus muscles) posteriorly and the anterior compartment (extensor digitorum longus) anteriorly. The superficial peroneal nerve is usually seen in this intermuscular fascial plane. Sliding distally towards the distal 1/3 of the leg the nerve emerges from deep in this fascial plane to sit just under the deep fascia of the leg (the fascia covering the superficial surface of the muscles). It is easiest imaged in this location, where it stays for a short distance appearing as a small bunch of hypoechoic fascicles before exiting this intermuscular fascial plane. After piercing the deep fascia of the leg, the nerve continues distally on the superficial surface of the deep fascia or in the subcutaneous tissues where it can appear as a flattened string of small hypoechoic fascicles which then divide into branches.
Practical tips: pass the needle IP from anterior or posterior depending on your position. Block this nerve before it pierces the deep fascia or immediately after to ensure block before branching occurs. Use smaller gauge needles for ankle blocks in awake patients for patient comfort.

notes.full_text:
Saphenous nerve (ankle) notes
Indications: analgesia to medial malleolus and medial foot. Usually combined with other nerve blocks to perform an ankle block of entire foot.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 3-5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: nerve injury, vessel puncture.
Sonoanatomy tips: place probe transversely over the anteromedial ankle with very light pressure (and use a tourniquet if able) to identify the greater saphenous vein. Slide the probe proximally and distally along the vein to try and identify the saphenous nerve branches running in close proximity. They may be divided around the vein. They are usually very small and very difficult or impossible to image unless a very high frequency transducer is used.
Practical tips: If the nerve is not identified (the usual situation) insert the needle in plane from the posterior end of the probe to surround the vein and fill the fascial plane posterior to vein with LA.
Another reliable way to block the saphenous nerve is with an adductor canal block.
Saphenous nerve block can be omitted from "ankle blocks" for surgery on the toes or lateral foot.

notes.full_text:
Indications: analgesia to lateral side of foot. Usually combined with other nerve blocks to achieve ankle block of entire foot.
Positioning: lateral with operative side uppermost. Supine with foot elevated on support also possible.
Volume: 3-5 mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: nerve injury, vessel puncture.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely over the posterolateral leg just proximal to the lateral malleolus. Identify the peroneus brevis anteriorly, the achilles tendon posteriorly and the small saphenous vein in the fascial plane between them. Use a tourniquet and light probe pressure to avoid compressing the vein. The nerve is small and difficult to see but is usually hyperechoic and near the vein. Tracing the nerve and the small saphenous vein proximally will show the nerve and vein moving posteriorly to run subcutaneously superficial to the Achilles tendon.
The nerve can also be traced down from the posterior upper/mid-calf where it exits the deep fascia between the medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius to then travel distally, with the small saphenous vein, in the subcutaneous tissues over Achilles tendon and then laterally towards the lateral malleolus.
The nerve can also be traced further distally, posterior to the lateral malleolus and into the lateral foot, continuing to be accompanied by the small saphenous vein.
Practical tips: in thin patients with a depression between the achilles tendon and lateral malleolus a small probe or “floating” the probe in lots of gel can help with probe contact. Alternatively block the nerve at a more proximal location in the postero-lateral calf subcutaneous tissues, or in the posterior leg after it pierces the deep fascia, emerging from the between the heads of gastrocnemius. Use smaller gauge needles for patient comfort when performing ankle blocks in awake patients. Pass the needle IP from either end of the probe or OOP, surrounding the small saphenous vein with LA if the nerve cannot be seen.

notes.full_text:
Erector spinae plane notes
Indications: unilateral chest wall analgesia e.g. rib fractures, thoracotomy, breast surgery.
Positioning: sitting (fatigue of probe holding arm more likely due to lack of ability to rest it on bed or patient), lateral (most comfortable for patient and allows sedation or GA), or prone (easiest for proceduralist if patient can comfortably lie prone preop).
Volume: 20-30 mL.
Side effects: weakness of erector spinae muscles.
Complications: pneumothorax, LAST, sympathetic block, epidural spread.
Sonoanatomy tips: start with the probe in a sagittal, paramedian plane on the posterior chest wall 10-15cm lateral to the spine. Identify the rounded hyperechoic ribs and the pleura sliding deep to the ribs. If you cannot see ribs ensure you are not over the scapular. Flexing the arm across the chest will move the scapular laterally.
Slide slowly medially and the pleura and ribs will get progressively deeper, then they will transition to the slightly more superficial, squared off appearance of the transverse processes with pleura no longer visible. To image the pleura deep to the transverse processes the probe needs to be directed laterally. (This is because the pleura is diving deep and the angle of insonation of the US beam needs to be perpendicular to the pleura to get a good reflection).
Repeat this process until you are confidently identifying the transition from ribs to transverse processes: slide back laterally to the more easily imaged curved ribs with easy to see pleura deep to them, then slide medial again looking for the ribs and pleura to dive away deep and the transition to the transverse processes and the pleura that then requires lateral tilting of the probe to image.
At levels T2 to T5, 3 superficial muscle planes will be seen: trapezius, rhomboid major and erector spinae muscles. Caudad to T5 level only 2 superficial muscle layers are present: trapezius and erector spinae.
The muscles immediately superficial to the transverse processes are the erector spinae. The target plane is deep to the erector spinae muscles and superficial to the transverse processes.
Practical tips: insert the needle in plane from either end of the probe. Aim for a cephalad or caudad edge of the transverse process. Hit the bone to confirm your location if required. It can be difficult to penetrate the fascia on the deep side of the erector spinae when it is impinged against the bone by the needle. Injecting at this point can therefore often result in LA spreading into the deep part of the muscle instead of into the fascial plane deep to the muscle.
Walking the needle tip off one end of the transverse process allows the needle tip to tent and then pop through the fascia on the deep side of the erector spinae muscle. Inject a small amount to identify the correct spread pattern (it is important to be deep to the fascial plane on the deep side of the erector spinae muscles, and spread across the top of the transverse processes in the cephalad-caudad direction). If LA is seen to form a rounded blob or laminate in the muscle stop injecting and reposition the needle tip. A small amount of spread back along the needle and into the muscle is not uncommon. Injection deep to this plane into the intertransverse tissue complex also results in an effective block but may not spread over as many levels.
This block can be performed bilaterally, and at multiple levels, however due to large volumes take care with total LA dose. This is a more superficial, easier and lower risk block than a paravertebral. It is a good option if a paravertebral is considered too difficult, eg in obesity or practitioner inexperience, or when the risk of pneumothorax is not justified.
Useful surface anatomy: most prominent spinous process is usually C7, spine of scapula is at T3 level. angle of scapular is at T7 level.
Useful sonoanatomy: rhomboid major (making 3 superficial muscle layers) only seen at T2-T5.

pneumothorax, LAST, sympathetic block, epidural spread.
Sonoanatomy tips: start with the probe in a sagittal, paramedian plane on the posterior chest wall 10-15cm lateral to the spine. Identify the rounded hyperechoic ribs and the pleura sliding deep to the ribs. If you cannot see ribs ensure you are not over the scapular. Flexing the arm across the chest will move the scapular laterally.
Slide slowly medially and the pleura and ribs will get progressively deeper, then they will transition to the slightly more superficial, squared off appearance of the transverse processes with pleura no longer visible. To image the pleura deep to the transverse processes the probe needs to be directed laterally. (This is because the pleura is diving deep and the angle of insonation of the US beam needs to be perpendicular to the pleura to get a good reflection).
Repeat this process until you are confidently identifying the transition from ribs to transverse processes: slide back laterally to the more easily imaged curved ribs with easy to see pleura deep to them, then slide medial again looking for the ribs and pleura to dive away deep and the transition to the transverse processes and the pleura that then requires lateral tilting of the probe to image.
At levels T2 to T5, 3 superficial muscle planes will be seen: trapezius, rhomboid major and erector spinae muscles. Caudad to T5 level only 2 superficial muscle layers are present: trapezius and erector spinae.
The muscles immediately superficial to the transverse processes are the erector spinae. The target plane is deep to the erector spinae muscles and superficial to the transverse processes.
notes.practical_tips:
insert the needle in plane from either end of the probe. Aim for a cephalad or caudad edge of the transverse process. Hit the bone to confirm your location if required. It can be difficult to penetrate the fascia on the deep side of the erector spinae when it is impinged against the bone by the needle. Injecting at this point can therefore often result in LA spreading into the deep part of the muscle instead of into the fascial plane deep to the muscle.
Walking the needle tip off one end of the transverse process allows the needle tip to tent and then pop through the fascia on the deep side of the erector spinae muscle. Inject a small amount to identify the correct spread pattern (it is important to be deep to the fascial plane on the deep side of the erector spinae muscles, and spread across the top of the transverse processes in the cephalad-caudad direction). If LA is seen to form a rounded blob or laminate in the muscle stop injecting and reposition the needle tip. A small amount of spread back along the needle and into the muscle is not uncommon. Injection deep to this plane into the intertransverse tissue complex also results in an effective block but may not spread over as many levels.
This block can be performed bilaterally, and at multiple levels, however due to large volumes take care with total LA dose. This is a more superficial, easier and lower risk block than a paravertebral. It is a good option if a paravertebral is considered too difficult, eg in obesity or practitioner inexperience, or when the risk of pneumothorax is not justified.
Useful surface anatomy: most prominent spinous process is usually C7, spine of scapula is at T3 level. angle of scapular is at T7 level.
Useful sonoanatomy: rhomboid major (making 3 superficial muscle layers) only seen at T2-T5.

notes.full_text:
Indications: unilateral upper medial abdominal wall analgesia. Bilateral blocks usually performed to achieve midline, upper/middle abdominal wall analgesia. Ideal for periumbilical abdominal wall procedures.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 10-30 mL per side.
Side effects: rectus abdominus weakness.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, intra-abdominal viscus puncture, LAST.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe transversely at umbilical level or above. Identify rectus abdominus medially, the linear semilunaris and the three abdominal wall muscle layers laterally. Look for a double line along the posterior surface of rectus abdominus. This is likely the posterior rectus sheath and the transversalis fascia/peritoneum complex. The target plane is superficial to these, between the rectus muscle and the posterior rectus sheath (not between the parallel fascial planes). If only one fascial plane is seen on the posterior surface of rectus this is likely the posterior rectus sheath, transversalis fascia and peritoneum all together. The target plane is the same, being between muscle and the posterior rectus sheath. The superior epigastric vessels are usually seen running in this target plane.
Scanning cephalad, up to the subcostal area will show transversus abdominus extending further under rectus abdominus. Scanning caudally, below the umbilicus to the arcuate line (approximately 1/3 of the way from umbilicus to pubic crest) will show no double line as there is no posterior rectus sheath below this level. Only the peritoneum/transversalis fascia complex exists between rectus abdominus and peritoneal cavity below this level.
Practical tips: this block is best performed at umbilical level or above (due to lack of posterior rectus sheath below arcuate line). Does not provide any intra-abdominal visceral analgesia, only abdominal wall analgesia. Must be performed bilaterally to cover the midline. Use an IP technique from lateral or rotate probe to a sagittal, paramedian orientation and use an in plane technique from cephalad or caudad (popular approach for catheter insertion). Take care to avoid superior epigastric vessels running in this plane. For small periumbilical procedures 10mL per side is adequate. For large midline incisions from xiphisternum to below umbilicus use 30mL per side.

notes.full_text:
Cervical plexus (intermediate) notes
Indications: anaesthesia and analgesia to anterolateral neck and upper chest. Commonly used for carotid surgery, thyroid surgery, clavicle surgery and other superficial neck and upper chest procedures. Also used for shoulder surgery in addition to an interscalene block to block the supraclavicular nerves that innervate the "cape" of the shoulder.
Positioning: lateral, or supine with head turned to contralateral side.
Volume: 5-15 mL.
Side effects: nil with superficial (subcutaneous) approach to the superficial cervical plexus. Deeper needle insertion during this “intermediate” approach to the superficial cervical plexus ( the most popular US guided approach) may result in shortness of breath (phrenic block), hoarse voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve block) and arm weakness (brachial plexus block).
Complications: nerve injury, vessel puncture causing haematoma.
Sonoanatomy tips: this “intermediate” approach to the superficial cervical plexus is usually performed. Place the probe transversely on the lateral neck over the posterior edge of sternocleidomastoid midway between the sternum and the mastoid. Sliding the probe caudad and back cephalad look for the transverse processes. Identify C7 transverse process (absent anterior tubercle and vertebral artery visible) and C6 transverse process (wide foramen, prominent anterior "Chassaignacs" tubercle, vertebral artery not visible). ( See main menu item: "cervical spine transverse processes" for examples of this). Slide cephalad identifying C5 and C4 transverse processes becoming more superficial.
If cervical levels cannot be confidently identified via imaging the transverse processes, the carotid artery usually divides around C4 level (easily imaged) and the thyroid cartilage prominence is usually around C4/5 level (easily palpated).
This block is best performed at C4/C5 level. Identify the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid superficially at this level. The target is the plane between the deep side of sternocleidomastoid and the superficial surface of the deep muscles (middle scalene and levator scapulae). This space contains fat and the cervical plexus nerves and is contained by the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia which ensheathes sternocleidomastoid, and the prevertebral layer of the deep cervical fascia which covers the superficial surface of the deeper muscles. As you slide the probe cephalad and back caudad, branches of the cervical plexus may be seen travelling in this plane from antero-medially as they leave transverse processes, to postero-laterally where they wrap around the posterior boarder of sternocleidomastoid. The nerves are not usually easy to identify as they have a similar echogenicity to the connective tissue in this plane. However this target plane is easily identified.
Practical tips: insert the needle in plane around C4 level infiltrating the target plane deep to sternocleidomastoid from the posterior boarder of sternocleidomastoid to above the transverse processes. Surround any nerve like structures seen. Caution in severe respiratory compromised or contralateral phrenic palsy due to risk of phrenic block. Consider superficial (subcutaneous) cervical plexus block n this situation (subcutaneous injection only, superficial to the fascia that surrounds sternocleidomastoid).
For carotid surgery the glossopharyngeal nerve also needs to be blocked. This nerve runs inside the carotid sheath and is usually infiltrated by the surgeon under direct vision when the sheath is opened. Doing this ultrasound guided at the same time as this intermediate cervical plexus block has also been described but great care needs to be taken near these large vessels.
Deep cervical plexus block at C2-4 nerve root depth, blocks motor innervation of the neck muscles in addition to the sensory block provided by superficial cervical plexus blocks. However, the deep block has much greater risks and side effects, similar sensory block, and is rarely indicated.

notes.full_text:
Paravertebral (transverse) notes
Indications: unilateral analgesia to chest or abdominal wall. Sympathetic block also provides visceral analgesia. Commonly used for breast surgery, thoracotomy, rib fractures, renal and unilateral abdominal surgery.
Positioning: sitting or lateral.
Volume: 20 mL for single level block, less if multiple levels are being blocked.
Side effects: intercostal muscle weakness, abdominal wall muscle weakness, epidural spread.
Complications: pneumothorax, vessel puncture causing haematoma in deep incompressible location, nerve injury, sympathetic block causing hypotension.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe in the transverse orientation and image the thoracic spine. Place the spinous process on the edge of the image and slide the probe slightly cephalad and caudad to image the contour of the lamina rising to the transverse process with an acoustic shadow deep to it. Lateral and deep to the transverse process, pleura or rib are imaged (rib being a more superficial, static hyperechoic line with acoustic shadow deep, pleura being a slightly deeper, sliding hyperechoic line with lung artefact deep). Slide or tilt the probe slightly off the rib to image the pleura disappearing under the transverse process. Rotate the lateral end of the probe slightly caudally to align with the intercostal space, so you have no rib on your image, only pleura. Heel/toeing the probe to angle the beam slightly laterally will assist with imaging the pleura and needle. The internal intercostal membrane may sometimes be imaged as it extends from adjacent to the pleura to the transverse process. The target area is deep to the transverse process, and deep and medial to the internal intercostal membrane, superficial to pleura. A curvilinear probe will be useful if these structures are deeper than 4-5cm.
At levels T2 to T5, 3 superficial muscle planes will be seen, trapezius, rhomboid major and erector spinae muscles. Caudad to T5 level only 2 superficial muscle layers are present (trapezius and erector spinae).
Practical tips: lateral position allows for sedation and more patient comfort. Standing in front of the patient is often more ergonomic than behind. Single level block can cover 4-5 dermatomes. If more than this is required, it is better to block multiple levels. Insert the needle in plane from the lateral end of the probe. Seeing the pleura being depressed by LA injection is a good sign of being in the right plane.
If imaging is not adequate to perform the block under vision ( cannot image transverse process and pleura) the transverse process can be imaged in the parasagittal plane, and an erector spinae block performed (see "Erector spinae plane") or a landmark type of approach used by hitting transverse process with the needle and “walking off”, advancing a further 1cm and performing an intertransverse process block (see "Paravertebral sagittal"). Do not direct needle laterally as you are more likely to penetrate pleura laterally as it is more superficial. Medially the pleura dives deeper under the transverse process.
Spine of scapula is at T3 level.
Angle of scapular is at T7 level.

notes.full_text:
Paravertebral (sagittal) notes
Indications: unilateral analgesia to chest or abdominal wall. Sympathetic block also provides some visceral analgesia. Commonly used for breast surgery, thoracotomy, rib fractures, renal and unilateral abdominal surgery.
Positioning: sitting or lateral.
Volume: 20 mL for single level block, less if multiple levels are being blocked.
Side effects: intercostal muscle weakness, abdominal wall muscle weakness, epidural spread.
Complications: pneumothorax, vessel puncture with haematoma in deep incompressible location, nerve injury, sympathetic block causing hypotension.
Sonoanatomy tips: imaging the paravertebral space is difficult due to depth and predominance of bone shadows. With the probe in the median sagittal plane over the midline spinous processes slide laterally to identify transverse processes deep to erector spinae muscles. Slide further laterally and curved ribs with pleura between will be more easily imaged. Slide back medially and the pleura and ribs disappear deep and the more superficial, squared off appearance of the transverse processes come back into view. Slide laterally to ribs and back medially to transverse processes several times until you can confidently identify the transition. Keeping the transverse processes in view and tilting the probe laterally will help to image the pleura as it dives deep under the transverse processes. Do not be tempted to slide the probe back laterally where ribs and pleura are more easily imaged. Imaging transverse processes and pleura is essential for this block. The superior costotransverse ligament is usually very difficult to image and only occasionally seen.
At levels T2 to T5, 3 superficial muscle planes will be seen, trapezius, rhomboid major and erector spinae muscles. Caudad to T5 level only 2 superficial muscle layers are present (trapezius and erector spinae).
Practical tips: lateral position allows possibility of sedation and improved patient comfort. Insert the needle from the caudad end of the probe. Needle imaging will be difficult due to the steep angle of insertion and depth. Deeper than the transverse process needle imaging is usually poor. Injecting small volumes as you advance can help localise the needle tip (hydrolocation). The transverse process can be contacted to confirm location and then the needle can be walked off the transverse process. If the superior costotransverse ligament cannot be seen (the usual situation) advance the needle 1cm past the transverse process, or 2/3 the depth from the transverse process to the pleura. Injecting anywhere deeper than the transverse process but still superficial to the paravertebral space is called an intertransverse process block and should still be effective but may not spread over as many levels. Seeing the pleura being depressed by LA is a good sign of being in the paravertebral space. If the imaging or block performance is too difficult to ensure safe practice an alternative more superficial block, e.g. intertransverse process block or erector spinae block can be performed.
Spine of scapula is at T3 level.
Angle of scapular is at T7 level.

notes.full_text:
Superficial parasternal intercostal plane notes
Indications: anteromedial chest wall analgesia. Combined with serratus anterior plane or pectoserratus plane blocks for more complete breast analgesia or anterolateral hemithorax analgesia. Perform bilateral blocks for sternotomy and sternal fractures.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 20mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: pneumothorax, vascular puncture (internal thoracic vessels), pericardial puncture, LAST.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe in a sagittal paramedian orientation 1-2cm lateral to the mid sternum. Identify costal cartilages with pleura sliding visible deep to them. Slide the probe cephalad up to the clavicle. The first rib that is easily seen caudal to the clavicle is the 2
nd
th
 rib. Count down to the 4
 rib. Slide lateral to identify rib (shadow deep obscuring image of pleura) then back medial to identify transition to costal cartilage ( shadow deep not obscuring image of pleura). Identify pectoralis major as the most superficial muscle and the internal intercostal as the next deeper muscle between the costal cartilages. The internal thoracic artery may be seen in long axis deep to the intercostal muscles and the costal cartilages. Slide medially to identify the sternum then back about 1- 2cm lateral to perform the block.
Practical tips: this is a good block to combine with serratus anterior or pectoserratus blocks for medial coverage of breast or anterior hemithorax. This block has less risk of pneumothorax or puncture of internal thoracic vessels than the deep parasternal intercostal plane block. Pass the needle in plane from either end of the probe aiming to hit the costal cartilage or just walk off the edge of it to place the needle tip in the plane between pectoralis major and internal intercostal muscle. Getting the needle tip in the correct location to open up ( "unzip" ) an elliptical plane between the two muscles is essential to get good spread over multiple levels. Do not accept a LA spread in the muscle. The plane must be accessed and LA seen to spread over multiple levels. 20mL should spread over 3-4 levels. Performing the block at 2 levels (eg T 2/3 and T5/6 with 10mL at each level may get better spread). Must be performed bilaterally for sternum coverage.

notes.full_text:
Deep parasternal intercostal plane notes
Indications: anteromedial chest wall analgesia. Combined with serratus anterior plane or pectoserratus plane blocks for more complete breast analgesia or anterolateral hemithorax analgesia. Bilateral blocks are useful for sternotomy and sternal fractures.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 20mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: pneumothorax, vascular puncture (internal thoracic vessels) causing haematoma or damage to artery before harvest for CABG. Pericardium or cardiac puncture. LAST especially if combined with other blocks.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe in a sagittal, paramedian orientation 1-2cm lateral to the mid sternum. Identify costal cartilages with pleura sliding visible deep to them. Slide the probe cephalad up to the clavicle. The first rib that is easily seen caudal to the clavicle is the 2nd rib. Count down to the 4th rib. Slide lateral to identify rib (shadow deep obscuring image of pleura) then back medial to identify costal cartilage (pleura able to be imaged deep). Identify pectoralis major as the most superficial muscle and the internal intercostal as the next deeper muscle between costal cartilages. The internal thoracic artery may be seen on long axis deep to intercostal muscle and costal cartilage. Slide medial to identify sternum.
Between internal intercostal and pleura is the transversus thoracis muscle, it is usually only seen a few cm lateral to the lower third of the sternum, and is usually very thin. Rotate the probe into a transverse orientation between costal cartilages to more easily identify the transversus thoracis and the internal thoracic vessels in cross section. The target plane is deep to internal intercostal and superficial to transversus thoracis. The internal thoracic vessels also run in this plane.
Practical tips: perform this block with the probe in a transverse orientation, over an intercostal space adjacent to the lower half of the sternum. Pass the needle in plane from the lateral end of the probe to place the needle tip in the plane between internal intercostal muscle and transversus thoracis. Getting the needle tip in the correct location to open up an elliptical plane between the two muscles is essential to get good spread over multiple levels. Do not accept spread in the muscle. If the transversus thoracis cannot be identified access the plane deep to the internal intercostal where the vessels will be seen. This deep parasternal intercostal block likely has more risk of pneumothorax or puncture of internal thoracic vessels compared with the superficial parasternal intercostal block.

notes.full_text:
Interpectoral plane notes
Indications: analgesia to pectoralis major and pectoralis minor. Useful for subpectoral breast implants and subpectoral pacemaker insertions. Occasionally used with other nerve blocks for shoulder analgesia ( as lateral pectoral nerve contributes a small amount to shoulder innervation).
Positioning: supine, arm by side or abducted.
Volume: 10 mL.
Side effects: weakness of pectoral muscles.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury, pneumothorax.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe in a sagittal plane immediately below the mid clavicle in the deltopectoral groove. Image pectoralis major, pectoralis minor and axillary artery and vein deep to muscle layers. Tilting the probe medially will show the ribs, and pleura deep to the ribs. The rib deep to the vessels is the second rib. The target plane is between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor. Rotate the distal end of the probe towards the axilla 30-
 
45º sliding slightly inferolaterally along direction probe is pointing away from clavicle. Branches of the thoracoacromial artery and nerve like structures will often be seen running in the target plane between pectoralis major and minor.
Practical tips: this block targets the medial and lateral pectoral nerves only. It does not provide any cutaneous or subcutaneous anaesthesia. Insert the needle in plane from the cephalad end of the probe. Infiltrate the plane between the pectoral muscles targeting any nerve like structures seen. If targeting the lateral pectoral nerve for shoulder, AC joint or coracoid analgesia perform the block as proximal as possible to target the proximal branches of the lateral pectoral nerve.

notes.full_text:
Pectoserratus and interpectoral planes notes
Indications: analgesia to lateral breast, axilla, pectoral muscles and anterolateral chest wall.
Positioning: supine with arm abducted 45-90º.
Volume: superficial plane 10 mL, deep plane 20 mL.
Side effects: weakness of pectoral muscles, serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi. Some surgeons have objected to this block for breast cancer surgery as LA tracks to the axilla distorting fascial planes and there is a risk of needle trauma to malignant nodes.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury, pneumothorax, LAST.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe in a sagittal orientation in the deltopectoral groove immediately below the mid clavicle. Identify the pectoralis major, pectoralis minor and the axillary artery and vein. Tilt the probe medially to image the ribs and underlying pleura. The rib deep to the vessels is the 2nd rib. Rotate the distal end of the probe laterally towards the axilla 30-45º. Slide the probe inferolaterally along the direction it is pointing towards the axilla. As you approach the anterior axillary line identify the serratus anterior muscle appearing deep to pectoralis minor and immediately superficial to the ribs at the level of approximately the 4th rib. The target planes are between the two pectoral muscles (the thoracoacromial artery branches are usually seen in this plane ) and between pectoralis minor and serratus anterior ( the lateral thoracic artery or its branches may be seen in this plane). Use colour doppler to check for these vessels.
Practical tips: this blocks the medial and lateral pectoral nerves as per the interpectoral plane block and also blocks the lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves providing anterolateral cutaneous, subcutaneous and lateral breast analgesia. Also blocked are the intercostobrachial nerve innervating axilla and cutaneous upper medial arm, long thoracic nerve innervating serratus anterior, and the thoracodorsal nerve innervating latissimus dorsi.
Insert the needle from the cephalad end of the probe to deposit LA in the target planes between the pectoral muscles and between pectoralis minor and serratus anterior. Infiltrating the deeper plane first (between pectoralis minor and serratus anterior) will not compromise imaging of the superficial plane. These muscle planes can be very atrophic and thin in frail elderly women.
The medial half of the breast (anterior cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves) and the superior part of the breast just below the clavicle (supraclavicular nerves) are not covered by this block.

notes.full_text:
Superficial serratus anterior plane notes
Indications: analgesia to axilla, anterolateral chest wall and skin on upper medial arm (intercostobrachial nerve). Also popular for rib fracture analgesia.
Positioning: supine with arm abducted to 90º. Alternatively the arm across the chest can also work. Lateral position with arm in front of face also gives good access.
Volume: 20 mL.
Side effects: weakness of latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, nerve injury, pneumothorax.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe in a sagittal orientation immediately below the mid clavicle. The first rib that can be seen with ultrasound below the clavicle is the 2nd rib. Count ribs down from the 2nd rib in the mid clavicular line, follow the 5th rib laterally. Anteriorly the pectoralis major and minor muscles will be seen superficial to the ribs. In the mid-axillary line, the only muscle layer superficial to the ribs is the serratus anterior. Sliding the probe further posteriorly to the posterior axillary line will reveal the lateral edge of latissimus dorsi appearing superficial to the serratus anterior. The target plane is between latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior in the posterior axillary line. The thoracodorsal artery is often seen running in this plane. The pleura will be seen sliding with respiration deep to the ribs.
Practical tips: the nerves in this plane include the long thoracic nerve, the thoracodorsal nerve, the intercostobrachial nerve and the lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves. If standing at the patient’s head rotate the cephalad end of probe anteriorly to make needle insertion from the cephalad end easier. If standing at patients’ ipsilateral hip do not rotate the probe and insert needle from caudad end of probe. A deeper block between serratus and rib has also been described (deep serratus anterior plane block) but may not spread over as many levels as the plane superficial to serratus anterior. This block can also provide analgesia to the upper lateral abdominal wall by performing the block a few levels lower. This block has become popular for rib fracture analgesia however its mechanism of action for this is still unclear.

notes.full_text:
Subcostal TAP (upper) notes
Indications: analgesia to unilateral upper abdominal wall.
Positioning: supine
Volume: 20 mL per side.
Side effects: weakness of abdominal wall muscles.
Complications: LAST, perforation of intraperitoneal structures, vessel puncture causing haematoma.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe parallel and immediately caudad to the costal margin, as close to the xiphisternum as possible. Identify the rectus abdominus muscle and linear alba. Slide the probe laterally along the costal margin to identify the lateral edge of rectus abdominus, the linear semilunaris, and the 3 abdominal wall muscles lateral to this point. The transversus abdominus is the deepest, thinnest and most hypoechoic muscle layer. At this upper subcostal level the transversus abdominus usually extends medially under the linear semilunaris and under the lateral portion of rectus abdominus. The target plane is between rectus abdominus and transversus abdominus, as cephalad and medial as possible. The superior epigastric vessels run through this plane and are commonly seen.
Practical tips: insert the needle from either end of the probe. Keep the probe parallel to the costal margin. Use a long needle, and a hydrodisection technique to spread LA to block as many intercostal levels as possible eg T7-T10. Beware of superior epigastric vessels which run in this plane. The target plane is the plane immediately superficial to transversus abdominus. Medial to the linear semilunaris the transversus abdominus extends under rectus abdominus in this upper part of the abdomen. Lateral to linear semilunaris the transversus abdominus extends deep to internal and external oblique. Bilateral blocks are required for midline incisions. These blocks can be combined with subcostal TAP lower blocks for incisions extending just below the umbilicus. Because of the very large volume required caution with dosing is essential to avoid LAST.

notes.full_text:
Subcostal TAP (lower) notes

Positioning: supine
Volume: 20 mL per side.
Side effects: weakness of abdominal wall muscles.

Ultrasound tips: place the probe parallel and immediately caudad to the costal margin, as close to the xiphisternum as possible. Identify the rectus abdominus muscle. Slide the probe laterally along the costal margin to identify the linear semilunaris at the lateral edge of rectus abdominus and the 3 abdominal wall muscles lateral to this point. The target plane is the plane immediately superficial to transversus abdominus. This may be between rectus abdominus and transversus abdominus more cephalad (for a subcostal TAP upper block), between linea semilunaris and transversus abdominus or between external oblique and transversus abdominus the more lateral you move. Because of the very large volume required when combining TAP blocks, caution with dosing is essential to avoid LAST.

notes.full_text:
Midaxillary TAP notes
Indications: analgesia to the unilateral lower abdominal wall.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 20 mL per side.
Complications: bowel puncture, LAST, vessel puncture causing haematoma.
Side Effects: weakness of abdominal wall muscles.
Ultrasound tips: place the probe in a transverse orientation on the anterior abdominal wall at umbilicus level. Identify the rectus muscle medially with peritoneum and peristaltic movements of small bowel deep to it. Sliding the probe laterally identify, linear semilunaris, then the three abdominal wall muscle layers ( external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominus). Slide further laterally to the mid-axillary line between costal margin and iliac crest. The transversus abdominus muscle is the deepest, the thinnest and most hypoechoic of the 3 muscles. Tilting the probe back and forth can demonstrate the muscle fibres of external oblique and internal oblique running in opposite directions. Gas containing large bowel can usually be seen deep to the transversus abdominus in this lateral location. The target plane is between transversus abdominus and internal oblique.
Practical tips: insert the needle from the anterior end of the probe. Place the US machine across the other side of the patient. With some experience both sides can usually be performed whilst standing on one side of the patient. These blocks can be combined with subcostal TAP blocks for incisions extending up to and above the umbilicus, however because of the very large volume required, caution with dosing is essential to avoid LAST.
This midaxillary TAP technique (the first described TAP technique) covers very few dermatomes. Often just T11 and T12. A better approach is to slide slightly anterior and rotate the probe 45º to align with the costal margin aiming to spreads LA over more dermatomes. See subcostal TAP lower.

notes.full_text:
Ilioinguinal & iliohypogastric nerves notes
Indications: unilateral analgesia to cutaneous area of lower anterior abdominal wall just above inguinal ligament (iliohypogastric). Cutaneous area upper medial thigh and part of genitals (ilioinguinal). Often used for inguinal hernia, orchidopexy, or hydrocele surgery.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 5-10mL.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: puncture of bowel, intravascular injection causing haematoma, femoral nerve block resulting in quadriceps weakness.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe along a line between the ASIS and the umbilicus with the lateral edge of the probe over the ASIS. Toe the probe (push medial end deeper than lateral end i.e., push down with fingers and rest up with thumb) and slide slightly caudally to direct the ultrasound beam slightly laterally towards the ilium. Identify the 3 abdominal wall muscles: external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominus. Deep and medial is peritoneum, deep and lateral is iliacus and then the ilium with its acoustic shadow. External oblique may be only a fascia in this area, which can cause difficulty with correctly identifying the 3 abdominal wall muscles. Scan cephalad and laterally to confirm external oblique, then back again to observe if it transitions to a fascial layer. The nerves most commonly lie between the transversus abdominus and internal oblique, but variations are common. The nerves are often very close to the ilium at the ASIS level, and they will travel medially as you scan caudally. Blood vessels (branches of the deep circumflex iliac artery) often travel with the nerves and can aid in identification.
Practical tips: use an IP technique with the needle from the lateral end of the probe. If the nerves cannot be seen infiltrate the fascial plane between transversus abdominus and internal oblique as close to ASIS as possible. If the nerves are very close to the ASIS a needle trajectory from lateral may not be possible in which case trace the nerves further distally or an in plane approach from medial or an OOP approach can be used.

notes.full_text:
Anterior quadratus lumborum notes
Indications: unilateral abdominal wall analgesia, possibly some visceral analgesia and hip analgesia.
Positioning: lateral
Volume: 20-30 mL per side.
Side effects: weakness of abdominal wall muscles.
Complications: renal or other visceral puncture, vascular puncture causing haematoma in deep incompressible location, LAST, leg weakness if spread to lumbar plexus occurs.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe transversely on the lateral abdomen between iliac crest and costal margin in the mid axillary line. Ensure depth set adequately to image vertebrae (usually at least 10 cm). Slide the probe slightly posteriorly and rock the probe slightly in the anterior-posterior plane to image vertebrae. Once a vertebra is imaged then slide the probe slightly in a cephalad-caudad direction to image a transverse process. Next adjust the depth to place the vertebra towards the bottom of your screen so as to optimize imaging of the muscles above the transverse process.
The quadratus lumborum is usually an inverted triangular shaped muscle that appears more hypoechoic (darker) than the other muscles. Its deep apex inserts onto the transverse process tip. Superficial and anterior to it will be the thin abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominus). Superficial and posterior will be latissimus dorsi. Deep and anterior to quadratus is psoas, which is usually more hyperechoic than the other muscles. Psoas is immediately adjacent to the vertebral body and the anterior surface of the transverse process. Deep and posterior to quadratus is the erector spinae which is adjacent to the posterior boarder of the transverse process. The “Shamrock sign” is the three-leaf clover appearance of the psoas, quadratus and erector spinae (the leaves) around the transverse process (the stem).
The target plane for this anterior QL block is between quadratus lumborum and psoas. Anterior to quadratus and lateral to psoas a paranephric fat compartment is also usually seen adjacent to the target plane. The kidney can usually be seen descending into view if your patient takes a deep breath. The kidney is first surrounded by a perinephric fat compartment, then the renal fascia and then this paranephric fat compartment which usually extends adjacent to the target plane.
Practical tips: numerous quadratus lumborum blocks have been described and the role of each is currently uncertain. Bilateral blocks are required for any abdominal indication. This deeper anterior QL approach seems to be the most popular currently. This targets the plane between quadratus lumborum and psoas. This block approach requires the patient be rolled from one side to the other for bilateral blocks.
An advantage of the lateral quadratus lumborum block (see "quadratus lumborum lateral" ) is that it can be performed with the patient supine with a bolster under the hip (if they are not obese).

notes.full_text:
Lateral quadratus lumborum notes
Indications: unilateral abdominal wall analgesia, possibly some visceral analgesia and hip analgesia.
Positioning: supine, (a bolster under the hip can aid probe access). Lateral also possible.
Volume: 20-30 mL per side.
Side effects: weakness of abdominal wall muscles.
Complications: renal or other visceral puncture, vascular puncture causing haematoma in deep incompressible location, LAST, leg weakness if spread to lumbar plexus occurs.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a linear probe transversely on the lateral abdomen between iliac crest and costal margin in the mid axillary line. Image the three abdominal wall muscle layers. External oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominus. Slide the probe posteriorly following the 3 muscle layers. The transversus abdominus is usually the first layer to taper and end. The next muscle to appear posterior and deep to the tapered end of transversus abdominus is quadratus lumborum. The quadratus lumborum is usually an inverted triangular shaped muscle that appears more hypoechoic (darker) than the other muscles. Deep and anterior to quadratus psoas may be seen, which is usually more hyperechoic than the other muscles. Deep to the abdominal wall muscles and anterior to quadratus is a paranephric fat compartment. This paranephric fat compartment usually extends adjacent to the target plane. The target plane is the lateral corner of the quadratus muscle aiming to spread LA around quadratus.
Practical tips: numerous quadratus lumborum blocks have been described and it is currently uncertain the role of each. Bilateral blocks are usually required for any abdominal indication. An advantage of this lateral quadratus lumborum block is that it can be performed with the patient supine with a hip bolster (if they are not too obese).

notes.full_text:
Transversalis fascia plane notes
Indications: blocks L1 nerves: ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and maybe subcostal. Useful for iliac crest bone harvest, inguinal hernia, LUCS, other low abdominal wall/ groin incisions.
Positioning: supine or lateral.
Volume: 20 mL.
Side effects: weakness of abdominal wall muscles.
Complications: renal or other visceral puncture, vascular puncture causing haematoma in deep incompressible location, LAST, leg weakness if spread to lumbar plexus occurs.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a linear or curvilinear probe transversely on the lateral abdomen just above iliac crest in the mid axillary line. Image the three abdominal wall muscle layers; external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominus. Slide the probe posteriorly following the 3 muscle layers. The transversus abdominus is the thinnest and darkest and is usually the first layer to taper and end. The next muscle to appear posterior and deep to the tapered end of transversus abdominus is quadratus lumborum. The quadratus lumborum is usually an inverted triangular shaped muscle that appears more hypoechoic (darker) than the other muscles. Deep and anterior to quadratus lumborum the psoas may be seen, which is usually more hyperechoic than the other muscles. Deep to the abdominal wall muscles, anterior to quadratus and lateral to psoas a paranephric fat compartment is also usually seen. The kidney can be seen descending into view if your patient takes a deep breath. The kidney is first surrounded by a perinephric fat compartment, then the renal fascia and then this paranephric fat compartment. The peritoneal cavity is more anterior and bowel gas may be seen. The transversalis fascia cannot usually be seen as a separate fascial layer but runs on the deep side of transversus abdominus, and then the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum. Sometimes nerve like structures will be seen in this area. The target plane is just deep to the tapered end of transversus abdominus, superficial to the pararenal fat compartment.
Practical tips: More distal blocks of the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves in the TAP plane will miss the proximal branches that innervate the iliac crest. So for iliac crest bone graft this more proximal approach is recommended. An in plane needle approach from anterior is usually performed.

notes.full_text:
Paediatric brachial plexus axillary notes
Indications: anaesthesia to hand. Anaesthesia to forearm if musculocutaneous and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves are successfully blocked (sometimes missed with this technique due to incorrect identification and anatomical variations). Analgesia to whole arm below the shoulder joint.
Positioning: supine with arm abducted 90º, or with hand tucked under head.
Volume: 0.3-0.5 mL/kg 0.2-0.375% ropivacaine or 0.25% levobupivacaine/bupivacaine.
Side effects: muscle weakness of arm and hand.
Complications: vessel puncture, intravascular injection and LAST, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe high in the axilla at the level of the pectoralis major/biceps groove, imaging the arm in a transverse view towards the humerus. Identify the axillary artery very superficially and the deeper, straight hyperechoic line of the conjoint tendon (from latissimus dorsi and teres major) which extends posterior to the artery from superficial to a deep anterior attachment on the humerus. Three nerves sit adjacent to the artery. The median nerve is usually superficial and anterior, the ulnar nerve superficial and posterior, and the radial nerve deep and posterior between the artery and the conjoint tendon. The smaller medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm may occasionally also be seen superficial to the artery, usually within the axillary sheath between median and ulnar nerves. The musculocutaneous nerve is usually more anterior (away from the artery, outside the axillary sheath), most commonly passing through the body of coracobrachialis to then run distally in the plane between biceps (superficial) and coracobrachialis (deep).
Highly variable anatomy exists in the axilla with the nerves and vessels, especially with the musculocutaneous nerve. Tracing the nerves up from their location in the arm will help with identification in the axilla. Tracing the musculocutaneous nerve more proximally will usually show it moving closer to the axillary artery, eventually becoming adjacent to the median nerve.
There are multiple veins in the axilla, usually compressed by probe pressure. Release the probe pressure to see these axillary veins.
Practical tips: use light probe pressure to avoid compressing the artery. Great care should be taken to avoid IV injection of LA into compressed veins. Release probe pressure to see where the veins are, but block is then usually performed with veins compressed. Aspirate and ensure LA spread in the tissues is observed with every injection. If you are not seeing the LA spread, you may be in a compressed vein. Tourniquet pain (mostly ischaemic muscle pain) is usually adequately analgesed with axillary blockade, despite the cutaneous area of the medial arm not being covered. The medial brachial cutaneous nerve and the intercostobrachial nerve that innervate the cutaneous area of the medial arm are travelling outside the axillary sheath in a more superficial and posterior location, so will not be blocked with this standard technique. The musculocutaneous nerve is also usually outside the axillary sheath at this level and with lots of anatomical variability so may be mis-identified and inadequately blocked. Tracing it proximally and distally is essential for correct identification.
Insert the needle in plane from an anterior location that allows all 4 nerves to be accessed and surrounded with LA. If the 4 nerves cannot be confidently identified, spreading LA around the artery, will usually block the median, ulnar and radial nerves (but spare the musculocutaneous nerve) and be sufficient for hand anaesthesia, and analgesia to the arm below the axilla.
This is the safest brachial plexus block as it avoids any risk of phrenic block or pneumothorax, and any unintended arterial puncture can be easily managed with compression.

notes.full_text:
Paediatric rectus sheath notes
Indications: unilateral upper medial abdominal wall analgesia. Bilateral blocks usually performed to achieve midline abdominal wall analgesia T8, T9, T10, T11. Ideal for periumbilical abdominal wall procedures.
Positioning: supine.
Volume:  0.2-0.3ml/kg/side. Ropivacaine 0.2% or levobupivacaine/bupivacaine 0.25%. (Max dose bupivacaine in fascial plane blocks 0.75mg/kg).
Side effects: rectus abdominus weakness.
Complications: vessel puncture causing haematoma, intra-abdominal viscus puncture, LAST.
Ultrasound Tips: place the probe transversely at umbilical level or above. Identify rectus abdominus medially, the linea semilunaris and the three abdominal wall muscle layers laterally. Look for a double line along the posterior surface of rectus abdominus. This is likely the posterior rectus sheath and transversalis fascia/peritoneum complex. The target plane is between the rectus muscle and the posterior rectus sheath not between the parallel fascial planes. If only one fascial plane is seen on the posterior surface of rectus this is likely the posterior rectus sheath, transversalis fascia and peritoneum together. The target plane is the same, being between muscle and the posterior rectus sheath. The superior epigastric vessels are usually seen running in this target plane. Scanning cephalad to the subcostal area will show transversus abdominus extending further under rectus abdominus. Scanning caudally below the umbilicus to below the arcuate line (approximately 1/3 of the way from umbilicus to pubic crest) will show no double line as there is no posterior rectus sheath below this level. Only the peritoneum/transversalis fascia complex exists between rectus abdominus and peritoneal cavity below this level.
Practical Tips: this block is best performed at umbilical level or above (due to lack of posterior rectus sheath below arcuate line). Does not provide any intra-abdominal visceral analgesia. Must be performed bilaterally to cover the midline. Use an IP technique from lateral or rotate probe to a para-sagittal orientation and use an in plane technique from cephalad (popular for catheter insertion). Take care to avoid superior epigastric vessels running in this plane. Intramuscular injections are commonly observed requiring needle repositioning. Ensure your LA is opening a plane between the muscle fibres and the posterior rectus sheath, and not intramuscular.

notes.full_text:
Paediatric quadratus lumborum notes
Indications: unilateral abdominal wall analgesia below the umbilicus, (possibly some visceral analgesia and hip analgesia).
Positioning: lateral is easiest, supine with a bolster under the hip to aid probe access is also possible.
Volume: 0.2- 0.4ml/kg/side. 0.2% ropivacaine or 0.25% levobupivacaine/bupivacaine. (Maximum dose of bupivacaine in fascial plane blocks 0.75mg/kg.)
Side effects: weakness of abdominal wall muscles.
Complications: renal or other visceral puncture, vascular puncture causing haematoma in deep incompressible location, LAST, leg weakness if spread to lumbar plexus occurs.
Sonoanatomy tips: place a linear probe transversely on the lateral abdomen between iliac crest and costal margin in the mid axillary line. Image the three abdominal wall muscle layers. The next muscle to appear posterior and deep to the tapered end of transversus abdominus is quadratus lumborum. The quadratus lumborum is usually an inverted triangular shaped muscle that appears more hypoechoic (darker) than the other muscles. Deep and anterior to quadratus the psoas may be seen, which is usually more hyperechoic (brighter) than the other muscles. Deep to the abdominal wall muscles and anterior to quadratus is a paranephric fat compartment. This paranephric fat compartment usually extends adjacent to the target plane. The target plane is the lateral corner of the quadratus muscle aiming to spread LA around quadratus.
Practical tips: numerous quadratus lumborum blocks have been described and it is currently uncertain the role of each. Bilateral blocks are required for any midline incisions. Needle approaches from the posterior end of the probe keeps the needle trajectory further away from intraperitoneal structures.
