notes.full_text:
Paediatric caudal notes
Indications: epidural anaesthesia and analgesia to sacral, lumbar, and low thoracic dermatomes. Suitable for most surgery (general, urology, orthopaedics) at or below the umbilicus.
Positioning: lateral, or prone.
Volumes: 0.5ml/kg for sacral and low lumbar dermatomes (genital and lower limb surgery), 1ml/kg for high lumbar and low thoracic dermatomes (inguinal and periumbilical surgery), ropivacaine 0.2% or levobupivacaine/ bupivacaine 0.25%. (Maximum volume of bupivacaine 0.25% is 1ml/kg).
Side effects: leg weakness, hypotension from sympathetic block, urinary retention (very rare in non toilet trained child).
Complications: vascular puncture causing haematoma, intravascular injection, nerve injury, dural puncture, high spinal, LAST.
Sonoanatomy tips: start with transverse imaging just cephalad to the natal cleft scanning cephalad and caudad to identify the sacral cornua, sacral hiatus and confirm normal anatomy. The two cornua with underlying acoustic shadows stand out like eyes on a frog’s head. Between the two bony prominences of the cornua the echogenic posterior sacrococcygeal ligament is seen with the deeper more markedly echogenic sacral body being the most prominent white line. Between these two echogenic surfaces is the more hypoechoic sacral hiatus and caudal epidural space.
The probe is then rotated into a median sagittal orientation to image the midline sacral crest, sacral bodies and posterior sacrococcygeal ligament in long axis. The dural sac will be seen as a dark pointed structure in the sacral canal ending at S2 or S3 in neonates and infants. Caudal to the dural sac strands of the filum terminale or cauda equina may be seen in the sacral epidural fat extending to the coccyx. The coccyx may not have started to ossify in infants so may appear as a hypoechoic structure only without the hyperechoic cortex seen on the sacral bodies.
Practical tips: insert the needle in plane from the caudal end of the probe. Keep a superficial trajectory to pop through the sacrococcygeal ligament, into the caudal epidural space. Advance slightly into the sacral canal. Ensure needle tip and dural sac are kept in view to reduce the risk of dural puncture. Aspirate carefully to exclude intravascular placement in epidural vessels. Injection should show LA spreading cephalad in the sacral canal around the dural sac. Compression of the dural sac is often seen during injection with displacement of the dura mater ventrally away from the ligamentum flavum.

notes.full_text:
Paediatric penile nerves notes
Indications: procedures on the penis.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 0.2ml/kg ropivacaine 0.2% or levobupivacaine/ bupivacaine 0.25%.
Side effects: nil.
Complications: vascular puncture causing haematoma, injury to corpus cavernosum or spongiosum, intravascular injection, nerve injury, urethral injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: imaging the penis transversely (either dorsally or ventrally) will show the 3-leaf clover appearance of the two corpus cavernosum (dorsally) and the corpus spongiosum (ventrally). These hypoechoic structures are each immediately covered by the hyperechoic tunica albuginea. Within the centre of each corpus cavernosum the deep central artery is often seen. The urethra, within the corpus spongiosum, is collapsed and not usually seen.
On the dorsal side of the cavernosum a deep dorsal vein, with dorsal arteries on each side can be seen superficial to the tunica albuginea. The dorsal penile nerves are not clearly seen but run adjacent to the dorsal arteries.
The deep (Buck’s) fascia covers these deep dorsal vessels and dorsal nerves and continues around the cavernosum and spongiosum.
Superficial to the deep fascia on the body of the penis is a superficial dorsal vein, a fat layer, a superficial fascia, subcutaneous fat and skin.
Imaging and block performance, however, is usually performed at the level of the distal root of the penis. At this level the superficial fascia extends laterally rather than encircling the penis as it does on the body of the penis.
Imaging in the sagittal plane at the distal root of the penis will show the corpus cavernosum in long axis diving deep into the sub-pubic space. Cephalad to this the acoustic shadow of the pubic symphysis is seen with rectus abdominus/linea alba cephalad and attaching to the pubis. The membranous layer of the superficial (Scarpa’s) fascia forms a roof over a triangular subpubic space between the pubic symphysis and the deep fascia (Buck’s) covering the corpus cavernosum.
Superficial to the pubis and the distal part of the linea alba, the fundiform ligament forms from the membranous layer of the superficial (Scarpa’s) fascia. In the superficial, cephalad portion of the subpubic space this fundiform ligament is initially a midline structure but quickly divides into two, to diverge and form a sling that passes laterally around and underneath the distal root of the penis, suspending it towards the pubis.
Deeper in the subpubic space a midline suspensory ligament extends from pubis to the deep penile (Buck’s) fascia.
Practical tips: There are currently 3 approaches to the US guided penile block:
1)   Transverse dorsal.
This approach is easy to position the probe but the relevant anatomy gets squashed under the probe so identifying the fascial planes and vessels becomes difficult. It is also awkward to insert the needle in plane under the probe into the very superficial space. Light probe pressure, a short high frequency linear probe, and positioning the target under the near end of the probe can help. Injecting above or below the deep (Buck’s) fascia have both been used successfully. Injecting superficial to the deep fascia reduces the risk of neurovascular injury. Although the fundiform ligament (a bilateral "sling" at this level) is not usually seen, as it is a loose fibrofatty structure, lateral LA spread may appear contained by this structure. A subcutaneous local anaesthetic wheal on the ventral side of the base of the penis is also required to block the perineal branches of the pudendal nerve.
2)   Transverse ventral.
The probe positioning under the penis is not as convenient as the dorsal approach but the relevant anatomy is not squashed and is a bit further from the probe which makes needle insertion and finding the relevant planes easier and safer. Injecting a subcutaneous local anaesthetic wheal on the ventral side of the base of the penis first, to block the perineal branches also provides a useful acoustic window and spacer to image through. Inverting the image on the ultrasound screen makes image interpretation easier. Take care not to rotate the penis when applying traction as this will rotate the landmarks making block performance more difficult. Injecting above or below the deep (Buck’s) fascia have both been used successfully. Superficial to the deep fascia reduces the risk of neurovascular injury. Although the fundiform ligament (a bilateral "sling" at this level) is not usually seen, as it is a loose fibrofatty structure, lateral LA spread may appear contained by this structure.
3)   Sagittal.
The ergonomics of probe and needle handling are easiest with this approach although the relevant anatomy is a little harder to understand and image. The corpus cavernosum in long axis, pubic symphysis and the superficial fascia are the landmarks outlining the targeted subpubic space. The cephalad, midline fundiform ligament fibres are often seen in the superficial cephalad part of this subpubic space before they diverge from the midline to form a sling bilaterally around the penis, suspending it towards the pubis. Place LA deep to the superficial fascia, caudad to the pubic symphysis, and cephalad but close to the deep fascia of the penis. Either in plane or out of plane needle approaches can be used. A subcutaneous local anaesthetic wheal on the ventral side of the base of the penis is also required to block the perineal branches.


Deeper in the subpubic space the midline suspensory ligament may also limit LA spread, which is why bilateral injections have been commonly used for the landmark technique. However, single injections have also been used successfully. Diffusion of LA across this suspensory ligament and the deep (Buck’s) fascia appears likely.
The 3 ultrasound guided approaches described above are intended to be superficial to the midline suspensory ligament, between the bilateral “sling” portions of the fundiform ligament, in the most superficial part of the subpubic space.
As with all ultrasound guided nerve blocks, LA spread should be able to be visually monitored and injection location modified, if required, to achieve the desired pattern of spread.

notes.full_text:
Paediatric femoral nerve notes
Indications: analgesia to hip, femoral shaft, and knee. Combine with a sciatic block for more extensive analgesia or for anaesthesia to leg and foot.
Positioning: supine.
Volume: 0.2-0.5ml/kg 0.2% ropivacaine or 0.25% levobupivacaine/bupivacaine.
Side effects: quadriceps weakness.
Complications: vascular puncture causing haematoma, intravascular injection, nerve injury.
Sonoanatomy tips: place the probe in a transverse orientation in the inguinal crease over the femoral vessels. Identify the femoral vein and artery. Stay as proximal as possible. Nerve imaging difficulty is usually due to scanning too distally as the femoral nerve quickly flattens and divides into multiple branches a few centimetres distal to the inguinal ligament. If the common femoral artery has divided into its deep (profunda) and superficial (subsartorial) branches, imaging is too distal.
Immediately deep and lateral to the artery you will see a large hypoechoic muscle, the iliopsoas. On the superficial surface of the iliopsoas is a bright hyperechoic fascia, the fascia iliaca, that runs medially, deep under the artery. The more superficial fascia that runs superficial to the artery is the fascia lata. The femoral nerve is usually seen as a flattened, spindle shaped, hyperechoic, honeycomb structure squashed between the iliopsoas muscle and the fascia iliaca lateral to the artery. Tilting the probe is required to make the nerve and fascia iliaca bright due to anisotropy. The echogenicity of the nerve is usually similar to the fascia iliaca making it difficult to distinguish the superficial margin of the nerve from the fascia iliaca. The hypoechoic fascicles in the nerve are the most distinguishing feature. LA injected in the plane just below the fascia iliaca hydrodisects the nerve from the fascia iliaca making imaging the nerve much easier.
The superficial circumflex iliac artery may occasionally be seen branching from the femoral artery and running laterally as a linear hypoechoic structure superficial to the fascia lata.
Practical tips: in obese patients an assistant may be required to retract the abdominal pannus so the probe can image proximally enough in the inguinal crease (rarely an issue in paediatrics). Advance the needle from the lateral end of the probe to penetrate the fascia iliaca at the lateral edge of the nerve. Use colour doppler to exclude the superficial circumflex iliac artery being in your needle path. LA can be placed above and/or below the nerve but must be deep to the fascia iliaca. Ensure your LA is spreading under the fascial plane that runs deep to the artery, not superficial to it. The LA often tracts between branches of the nerve giving the appearance of the nerve separating into segments.
If the nerve is not confidently seen, placing LA deep to the fascia iliaca lateral to the artery will usually achieve a block.

notes.full_text:
Paediatric sciatic nerve popliteal notes
Indications: anaesthesia and analgesia to foot, ankle and leg. Covers most structures below the knee except those innervated by the saphenous nerve and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh. Combine with a saphenous nerve block (usually via an adductor canal block) for anaesthesia to foot, ankle and distal leg.
Positioning: lateral is most ergonomic but can be performed supine or prone.
Volume: 0.2-0.3ml/kg 0.2%ropivacaine or 0.25% levobupivacaine/bupivacaine.
Side effects: weakness of ankle flexors and extensors, and intrinsic muscles of the foot.
Complications: nerve injury, vessel puncture causing haematoma, LAST.
Ultrasound Tips: place the probe transversely in the popliteal fossa. Identify the popliteal vessels and tibial nerve immediately superficial to the vessels. Trace the tibial nerve proximally to identify the smaller common peroneal nerve coming from superficial and lateral to join the tibial nerve, together forming the sciatic nerve usually a few cm above the popliteal crease. Firm probe pressure helps imaging but remember to release probe pressure to check vein location. The nerves are highly anisotropic and require tilting of the probe, to optimize the image. The common peroneal nerve often appears to contain a single large (hypoechoic) fascicle. Flexing and extending the ankle, when possible, makes the nerves “seesaw” against each other aiding identification.
Practical Tips: this block is usually performed where the two nerves are first enclosed in a common sheath. The most proximal area of the bifurcation where a common sheath "slings" between the nerves. If this junction is too deep and imaging poor (due to obesity) the nerves can be blocked more distally where they are more superficial and easily imaged as two separate nerves. Small branches to the sural nerve may be seen coming from both nerves and may be missed if the block is performed too distally. Placing needle tip inside the common sheath where it appears stretching between the two nerves as they come together is a common technique providing a faster onset, more reliable block. Good imaging, needle control and injection technique is required to achieve this safely and avoid intraneural injection.
The saphenous innervation is to the skin on the medial leg including over the medial malleolus and sometimes distally to level of 1
st
 metatarsal head, and to some periosteum of the medial malleolus and medial ankle joint. The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh occasionally extends to innervate some cutaneous area on posterior proximal leg. These two nerves are not blocked with this technique.

notes.full_text:
Gastric antrum empty notes
Positioning: supine, slight head up, or right lateral decubitus (RLD).
Sonoanatomy tips: place a curvilinear probe, with an abdominal preset selected, in the sagittal plane in the epigastrium directly underneath the xiphisternum. Image the inferior liver edge superficially. Just deep to the liver edge the gastric antrum is usually seen. It appears as a rounded structure with a characteristic hypoechoic rim (from the thick muscularis propria). Once identified optimise your image by sliding slightly to the patients left or right side as required to image the large vessels deeper (aorta and IVC). Adjust the depth to put the large vessels and spinal cord towards the bottom of your image, and rotate the probe slightly to image the antrum in cross section (make the antrum image as round as possible. If you image it obliquely it will appear elliptical, elongated or cylindrical. Depending on the antrum contents it can have the following appearances:
Empty:
small, rounded, target like appearance. The lumen walls can abut each other or there is often a small amount of normal gastric secretions which appears as a hypoechoic centre. Folds of the antrum wall can often be seen.
• 
Clear fluid:
larger, depending on the amount of clear fluid. As the antrum becomes more distended, any folding of the wall disappears, and the wall can appear thinner as it distends and stretches. The hypoechoic muscularis propria layer persists as a characteristic feature of the antrum. The clear fluid appears as hypoechoic contents often with scattered hyperechoic bubbles floating throughout (the "stary night" appearance).
• 
Solids:
larger, depending on the amount of solids. As the antrum becomes more distended, any folding of the wall disappears, and the wall can appear thinner as it distends and stretches. The hypoechoic muscularis propria layer persists as a characteristic feature of the antrum. Solids have a more hyperechoic appearance compared with clear fluid. Depending on the nature of the solids it usually appears as a mixture of different sized and shaped hyperechoic structures or a heterogenous ground glass appearance.
• 
Air:
air is usually swallowed with ingested liquids and solids. Air will usually accumulate in the most superficial area of the antrum. Air appears as a bright hyperechoic line with dark hypoechoic shadowing underneath or with variably appearing laser like artefacts extending deep to the bottom of the image. This is because the ultrasound waves do not penetrate air so they are all reflected from the tissue/air interface producing the bright hyperechoic line with nothing visible deep.
• 
air usually indicates recent ingestion of antrum contents. Due to the air collecting superficially and shadowing deep to the tissue/air interface the contents of the antrum cannot be imaged. Recent ingestion is likely, and the nature of the contents cannot be determined.
• 
Practical tips: the antrum must be scanned in the RLD position before it can be called empty. This is because any gastric contents in the fundus will fall into the antrum in this position. A small amount of clear fluid (<1.5mLs/kg) seen in this position is consistent with normal gastric secretions and with a well fasted “empty” stomach. In the average adult this correlates with an antral cross sectional area (CSA) of <10cm2 in the RLD position at the level of the aorta.


CSA can be measured with most US machines and can be translated to a volume with the below charts from 
www.gastricultrasound.org

notes.full_text:
Transverse interlaminar low lumbar notes
Sonoanatomy tips: with a transverse orientation start low over the sacrum and slide slowly up over the lumbar spine. The appearance will alternate between a transverse interlaminar and transverse laminar image with each level. notes.full_text:
Transverse interlaminar mirror image artefact notes
Sonoanatomy tips: Occasionally with good transverse interlaminar views a mirror image artefact of the posterior complex is seen deep to the anterior complex causing confusion. This is due to the fluid filled thecal sac sitting on the bright bone reflector of the vertebral body. The ultrasound waves pass easily through the fluid filled thecal sac with little attenuation and bounce between the anterior and posterior complex before returning to probe. This results in a mirror image of the posterior complex deep to the anterior complex. The same phenomena is often seen deep to the first rib when the subclavian artery sits on the first rib in a supraclavicular brachial plexus view. When this artefact appears it can create uncertainty as to what is the correct anterior and posterior complex. Useful tips for correct identification are:
being aware this artefact can sometimes appear,
• 
the anterior complex will usually be the brightest and widest image as it is a flat bony reflector deep to a fluid filled sac,
• 
the posterior complex image is from curved ligamentous structures so will usually be less bright, often curved, often not seen at all,
• 
the mirror image artefact, if present, will usually be less bright than the anterior complex, and appear equal distance deep to the anterior complex, as the posterior complex is above,
• 
rotating the probe and obtaining a sagittal oblique interlaminar view and comparing depths can help as the posterior complex is usually more clearly seen with this view.
•

notes.full_text:
C7 & C6 transverse processes notes
Ultrasound tips: cervical spine levels can be determined by the shape of the C7 and C6 transverse processes. The C7 transverse process has an absent anterior tubercle which contrasts with the C6 transverse process which has a prominent anterior tubercle ( Chassaignac's tubercle ).
At C7 level the transverse foramen usually only transmits the vertebral vein so the vertebral artery and accompanying venous plexus is usually visible at this level. The vertebral artery and vein are enclosed in the transverse foramen of the anterior tubercles of C6 and above so are not easily seen above C7 level.
The anterior and posterior tubercles of C6 are more widely separated than those levels above. With ultrasound the C7 transverse process is usually the deepest with each transverse process above becoming progressively more superficial and the tubercles getting closer together.
Once C7 and C6 are identified the levels above can be identified by counting up. The common carotid artery usually swells into the carotid bulb at C5 level before dividing into internal and external carotids at C4 level.

notes.full_text:
Cricothyroid membrane sagittal notes
Sonoanatomy tips: transverse probe orientation is the easiest way for beginners to start, due to symmetry of structures on either side of the midline. Because the thyroid notch is usually the easiest to palpate structure on the front of the neck, start at the level of the thyroid cartilage. The thyroid cartilage appears as a bright hyperechoic inverted V shape with acoustic shadow deep to it. In males it is a more prominent and pointed V and in women it is a less prominent more rounded V. Strap muscles are seen on either side.
Slide the probe caudally from the thyroid cartilage and the inverted V of the thyroid cartilage disappears and after a short distance (~1-2cm) transitions to a less bright inverted U shape of the cricoid cartilage, with acoustic shadow deep often with some airway artifact appearing in this acoustic shadow. If you go too far caudad the more rounded, thinner tracheal cartilages with lots of reverberation artefacts deep and thyroid gland tissue laterally will appear.
Slide back and forth from the cricoid to the thyroid, inverted U to inverted V, until you are confident in identifying these two adjacent cartilages.
The cricothyroid membrane lies between these two cartilages. It appears as a bright hyperechoic line, (the trachea anterior mucosa-air interface) that is narrower than the thyroid or cricoid cartilages. When sliding cephalad from the cricoid it can appear as if the midline section of cricoid cartilage opens up to reveal the bright mucosa-air interface. The actual membrane is the less bright layer immediately superficial to the mucosa-air interface. This ultrasound appearance of a midline gap in the cricoid has been described as appearing like an “eroded ulcer” or “volcano crater”. Bright hyperechoic lines deep to the mucosa-air interface (brightest line) are reverberation artefacts.
Once the major structures are identified in the transverse orientation the probe can be rotated into a median sagittal orientation where all the important structures can be seen on the one image. The probe must be in a strict median sagittal position to get this image. The mucosa-air interface is the brightest hyperechoic line extending from the caudad end of the image to the thyroid cartilage. Sitting immediately superficial to this brightest line the tracheal cartilages appear as a line of black hypoechoic circles (the “string of black pearls” appearance). The most cephalad “black pearl” is much bigger than the rest. This is the cricoid cartilage. The next large hypoechoic shadow cephalad to the cricoid is the thyroid cartilage. The cricothyroid membrane stretches from the cricoid cartilage to thyroid cartilage, immediately superficial to the bright mucosa-air interface.
With experience clinicians may choose to go straight to the sagittal view.
Practical tips: airway US is recommended in patients where the cricothyroid membrane cannot be confidently palpated before an elective front of neck airway access or before any general anaesthesia where a front of neck access forms part of a rescue plan and the structures are not easily palpated. It is usually performed pre operatively and the CTM marked to assist the clinician if an emergency FONA becomes necessary.
